maintopic: FREIGHT RATES-INCREASES ORDERED BY TRANSPORT BOARD-AMENDMENT, MR. COLDWELL- SUBAMENDMENT, MR. BRACKEN

speechtext: The house resumed from1 Wednesday, April 14, consideration of the motion of Mr. Abbott for committee of supply, and the amendment thereto of Mr. Coldwell, and the amendment to the amendment of Mr. Bracken.

maintopic: FREIGHT RATES-INCREASES ORDERED BY TRANSPORT BOARD-AMENDMENT, MR. COLDWELL- SUBAMENDMENT, MR. BRACKEN
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, when the house rose yesterday at six o'clock I had pointed out that there were two phases to this issue of increased freight rates.

maintopic: FREIGHT RATES-INCREASES ORDERED BY TRANSPORT BOARD-AMENDMENT, MR. COLDWELL- SUBAMENDMENT, MR. BRACKEN
speechtext: Order.

maintopic: FREIGHT RATES-INCREASES ORDERED BY TRANSPORT BOARD-AMENDMENT, MR. COLDWELL- SUBAMENDMENT, MR. BRACKEN
speechtext:
I have pointed out that there are two phases to this issue of freight rate increases, namely, the general increase of 21 per cent across the board, and the question of equalization of freight rates across the country.
On April 7 the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell), who leads this group, put the following motion as reported at page 2743 of Hansard:
. . . this house is of the opinion that the failure of the government to defer the imposition of the increases in freight rates recently authorized by the board of transport commissioners is inimical to the best interests of the people of Canada; further this house is of the opinion that the government should reconsider this matter and take action to prevent the proposed increases from coming into effect at this time.
What the debate has been about since that motion was moved has been chiefly whether the present government at Ottawa should take the responsibility-

maintopic: FREIGHT RATES-INCREASES ORDERED BY TRANSPORT BOARD-AMENDMENT, MR. COLDWELL- SUBAMENDMENT, MR. BRACKEN
speechtext: Order. May I ask the hon. members to keep silent? I would ask the hon. member who has the floor if he will be kind enough to speak louder.

maintopic: FREIGHT RATES-INCREASES ORDERED BY TRANSPORT BOARD-AMENDMENT, MR. COLDWELL- SUBAMENDMENT, MR. BRACKEN
speechtext: Thank you; I shall do my best. Before I am through I believe I shall be able to make myself heard. I like to wind up slowly.

maintopic: FREIGHT RATES-INCREASES ORDERED BY TRANSPORT BOARD-AMENDMENT, MR. COLDWELL- SUBAMENDMENT, MR. BRACKEN
speechtext:
Speak up.
Freight Rates

maintopic: FREIGHT RATES-INCREASES ORDERED BY TRANSPORT BOARD-AMENDMENT, MR. COLDWELL- SUBAMENDMENT, MR. BRACKEN
speechtext:
You will hear presently more than you bargained for.
As I said, the debate so far has been on the motion of the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar. Later the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bracken) moved an amendment to the amendment which, for all practical purposes, is merely a paraphrased version of the original amendment. The debate has revolved around whether or not the government should take the responsibility of deferring the imposition of the new freight rates, or whether the matter should be shelved or passed on to some other body. I hold in my hand a clipping which was handed to me only today which I think indicates the wisdom of the plea which my leader made for deferring the imposition of these rates until further consideration is given to them and until the provinces have had an opportunity to put their case before the board, if reconsideration is to be given to them. The clipping refers to the situation at the port of Halifax. It is dated Halifax, April 14. I submit that this has a very strong bearing on what we have had to say in this house, because the dispatch says:
Provincial government and waterfront officials today protested anew against increased freight rates as they considered its latest ramification- diversion of vessels from this port to avoid long rail hauls for cargoes. First example of this was the freighter Martha Kleppe, which arrived here today from Suez with 3,100 tons of peanut products and other cargo, consigned to Hamilton, Ontario. When about 1,000 tons had been discharged, the consignees changed their instructions and ordered the ship to New York. From there the goods would be sent to a great lakes port. An hour later it was learned that the English Prince, also carrying a cargo from the far east, had been diverted from Halifax to Montreal to save rail charges.
President J. J. Campbell, of the longshoremen's association, said the two diversions were examples of "what is in the wind."
"If we lose the far east business, we might as well hang out the crepe," he said.
Here is one example, and perhaps one of the first, to show that the tax increase of 21 per cent may have a more upsetting effect so far as the maritime provinces are concerned than was intended. That is to say, the transportation system of the two railways in the mari-times may find that instead of increasing the revenue by increasing the rates, they may actually receive less revenue in the long run, because shipping will be diverted from its regular course to the waterways in order to avoid paying higher rates. What is true of the maritime provinces is, to a certain extent, also true of the central provinces. There happens to be truck competition in the two central provinces. There is water competition for the

maritime provinces. For these reasons the railways are faced with one of two alternatives. They have either to keep the rates low enough to compete with these other systems of transportation and face a deficit, or put their rates up in some other part of Canada to make up the difference in the revenue. The result will be that, if the railway companies decide not to go the full length of the increase in the two central provinces because of the competition, they will eventually, in order to keep the revenue up, have to place still higher rates on the four western provinces. All this goes to show that it is time the government took , an over-all view of the whole transportation system and took immediate steps to see that equalization and justice are given to all parts of Canada.
The suggestions made by my leader in the course of his speech following his motion have, to some extent, been already adopted by the government, although under very severe pressure-but not to the full extent that they would have been adopted had the private members of the party that supports the government, and who sit across the way, and who at the first instance had been in the rebel camp, not too quickly laid down their arms. I believe they had a great opportunity to force the hand of the government on this issue, and they certainly should have used it. Of course I realize that things have happened since the motion was moved. We are told that there was a most powerful caucus held by the Liberal party, and according to the Journal of April 14 it appears that the whip was used mercilessly and ruthlessly, and whipped into line those so-called rebels who threatened to jump the line. According to the Journal we find that they were told very bluntly, because this issue is such an embarrassing one, because the risk of an election at this time might prove disastrous, they had better support the government, "or else", regardless of whether or not they had to face the music when they got back home.

maintopic: FREIGHT RATES-INCREASES ORDERED BY TRANSPORT BOARD-AMENDMENT, MR. COLDWELL- SUBAMENDMENT, MR. BRACKEN
speechtext: Were you there?

maintopic: FREIGHT RATES-INCREASES ORDERED BY TRANSPORT BOARD-AMENDMENT, MR. COLDWELL- SUBAMENDMENT, MR. BRACKEN
speechtext:
Apparently there was somebody in on it, because I am now going to quote from the Journal, which says this, referring to the statement of the Prime Minister:
It had been his idea since 1945, he told his followers, that the government should live out its full term of office,-
A very desirable objective. I continue:
-delaying an appeal to the country until the spring of 1950.

Freight Rates
Then the report says this:
It was after this discussion that he discussed the government's position on the freight rates issue, bluntly telling the members they would have to fall into line.
Here is the real thing:
Should there be any deviation from party loyalty bringing an adverse vote, it would mean a general election on the unwanted freight rates issue.
I do not know whether he meant an unwanted issue or unwanted rates. Further down the article says this, to soften the blow a little bit:
The election would be the only possible course, and he warned his followers he believed the country would be "angry" and "resent" an appeal to it on the freight rates issue in view of the much more serious world situation.
I cannot conceive of the world situation being so serious at any time that it would prevent a government from submitting its stewardship to the judgment of the Canadian people. If the government feel that they are right on this issue, and would like confirmation of it from the Canadian people, I do not believe that they should use this subterfuge or a smoke-screen or any excuse to by-pass it and say to their followers: You will support the government because of the international situation, regardless of whether our domestic policies are right or wrong.
It is no secret that we have had two general elections in this country during the war, and the international situation then must certainly have been more serious than it is now. Yet at the present time, when the Prime Minister apparently feels that the issues are not favourable to the government, he warns his followers, You will support the government or take the consequences. I believe they will have to take the consequences in either event -if not now, at any rate later.
The minister also referred to the way in which the government treated the premiers of the provinces. The provincial governments made a very reasonable request asking that the government defer the putting into effect of the increase until they had had an opportunity to prepare and present their case on appeal. Instead of granting that very reasonable request, the government of course, in their famous order in council which was tabled in the house on April 7, told the premiers bluntly that they would do nothing of the sort.
I wish to quote briefly from an editorial which appeared recently in a newspaper which has recently begun publication. I refer to the Winnipeg Citizen, which to the best of my
knowledge and belief expresses an independent point of view. I quote:
Without a master hand at the controls, the government at Ottawa discloses an innate ability to take the wrong course. Latest of its maladroit moves must be considered the decision to refrain from delaying the enforcement of the 21 per cent rate increase permitted by the board of transport commissioners.
On April 24, the government is to meet the premiers of seven provinces to hear their representations on the matter.
Incidentally, the premiers have not yet appeared here; therefore the case has been prejudged. To continue:
There can seldom have been a more discourteous move on the part of a senior government than so to permit the subject of an appeal to be enforced before hearing the appellants' case. The premiers will meet to discuss an operation already settled and in effect. Is it to be supposed that Ottawa will reverse this fait accompli and thus create even more confusion?
It is doubtful if greater confusion is possible. The editorial goes on to say:
Operation "dropping the pilot" has not shown evidences of careful planning. In Mr. King's heyday there would not have been the series of tactical blunders perpetrated in the house and out of it in the past few months, seemingly the result of the lack of his masterful technique. Or is it that the government is old and tired?
I hope the electors will not allow the government to die of old age. No doubt they will take care of that. The point is, however, that this government, with perfect propriety, and I believe in perfect justice, could have given in to the plea of the premiers of the seven provinces and waited at least until they could prepare their appeal and take it to the proper body.
It is not only discourteous but it is taking an unfair advantage of any appellant when you have prejudged his case and handed him an accomplished fact before he has had an opportunity to lay the evidence before the judge.
I want to refer to the discrimination which exists between different parts of Canada in the matter of freight rates. Often in this house we have deplored, or those of us from western Canada have deplored, the fact that western Canada, which has so many varied resources, has not the secondary industry which it should have in order to develop those resources and convert them into finished products. We are being put in the position all *the time of having to produce our raw material and ship it east, paying freight rate on it, and then have it shipped back in finished form, paying freight rate on it again.
I believe the members of the house will agree when I say that one of the reasons for
Freight Rates

the lack of population in the west as compared with the central provinces is the fact that we have not been able to establish industry in our part of the country to the point that it should have been established by this time. One of the reasons for that is that the freight rate system works against any manufacturing industry in western Canada.
I have here some figures which I should like to put on Hansard. I will not put them all on, because we have been figured to death in the house in the last few days, but those that I am about to give are significant in that they show how the difference in the rates works against manufacturing in western Canada.
Let us take canned goods, for example. If you shipped canned goods from Vancouver to Calgary, a distance of 642 miles, the rate would be 98 cents per 100 pounds, whereas from Chatham, Ontario, to Thetford Mines, Quebec, which is 678 miles, a longer distance, the rate is only 45 cents per 100 pounds, or less than half the rate charged in the west.
Take cement. On a 300-mile haul the rate in western Canada or on the prairies is 24 cents per 100 pounds while in Ontario and Quebec it is only 19 cents.
Or take livestock. On a 300-mile haul on the prairies the rate is 30 cents per 100 pounds and in Ontario and Quebec it is 27 cents.
I have heard the hon. member for Medicine Hat (Mr. Wylie), which is in the province of Alberta, make the statement that if irrigation could be developed in his part of the province they could raise there vegetables which could compete with those produced in any part of Canada. I am not going to comment on the soundness of that statement, because I do not know. I take his word for it. But even if they could grow vegetables and can them there, with the freight rate system as it is operating against them1 they would have to pay more than twice the rate per 100 pounds to ship vegetables than is charged in the central provinces.
I want to make it clear that I am not joining in any criticism of the two central provinces. The people in Ontario and Quebec are not in the least responsible for the discrepancy in the freight rate system. That is something that is the responsibility and duty of the federal government, because we have a Department of Transport and a Minister of Transport-a genial minister, by the way-and it is their responsibility and duty to see to it that the transportation system of the country, and particularly the railroads, shall serve the needs of the Canadian people as conveniently

and as efficiently as possible and that the burden is distributed as fairly as it can be across the dominion.
Had the Minister of Transport accepted the motion moved by our leader in the first instance, most of this debate would have been unnecessary, but we have been put in the position in this house of having to get piecemeal concessions from the government by putting pressure after pressure upon it. That seems to be the only course which we can follow at the present time.
Earlier in this debate mention was made of certain rates on off-line hauls of grain, and today a question was asked about -rates on eggs, which again is evidence to show that the effect of the 21 per cent increase on branch lines in some parts of Canada is going to be even more serious than had been expected in the first instance.
The government has made the promise that it will submit to the board of transport commissioners, for another investigation, the whole question of equalization. It is doubtful whether, after the board has already sat for eighteen months, and after the government has had several opportunities to submit the question to the board, a submission at this time will bring any greater results than were achieved before.
I believe that we might be farther ahead in the long run if we were to admit that what is required is not another face-lifting job on this freight rate structure, but rather a major overhaul, and that the whole question should be submitted to an independent commission which would by-pass and perhaps to a certain extent forget the past history of the whole freight rate structure-all the prejudices and all the injustices that have crept in-and start from scratch t>o bring forth a plan which could be developed and brought into being.
On this point I wish to quote, again from the Winnipeg Citizen, a paragraph which I believe has a great deal of wisdom in it. It is as follows:
It is doubtful whether the present hoard, or any board appointed with the view of control of railway rates and practices, is competent to adjudicate the question so full of complexities outside the normal sphere of its authority. If the government wishes to carry the confidence of the country with it, it will appoint an absolutely independent commission of -a calibre equal to the importance of the issue and empower it to inquire into every phase and its full bearing upon public welfare.
I want to say that I agree with that paragraph. In other words, what is required now is an independent commissioner, perhaps a royal commission, which would take evidence

Freight Rates
across Canada apart altogether from the views of the railway companies or any interested persons, but based upon the welfare of the nation, and try to formulate a transportation plan which would work fairly in all parts of the dominion. I realize that it would not be an easy task, and it could not be done in a month or two. But from all appearances, even if it is handed to the board of transport commissioners, with all their experts and all the technical advice they can get, it is admitted that it may be a year, eighteen months or even longer before they can bring in their report or their judgment on the question of equalization.
There is something else to consider, and that is that we have reached the point in our transportation system where it is impossible to divorce railway transportation from truck, bus and boat competition. I think the whole system must now be taken as a unit for future purposes. In a modem country we can use all the forms of transportation we can lay our hands on, and I do not believe it will be necessary to displace any labour in the building up of a unified system of transportation. I think we can co-ordinate and synchronize the transportation of this country without displacing a single person, because we are still definitely in the expansionist stage of our transportation system:
We have been told in this house that we are now in the atomic age. On paper I suppose that is true, but much of our transportation is still just emerging from the horse and buggy stage. All we have to do is to go south across the boundary line to the United States, look at some of their forms of transportation, and compare them with some of ours. I am not saying that all of ours are in that stage. For example, we have the Trans-Canada Air Lines, which is almost a model of efficiency; we also have railway transportation which is of a high order. But much of our transportation is still in a backward stage of development. I think one of the reasons for that is the fact that in the past we have relied upon the principle of competition in a commercial way to provide transportation for this country. I believe that, up to a point, competition can be useful. but when it begins to interfere with the efficiency of the transportation system, when it is creating a chaotic condition or when it is getting to the point where competition becomes practically an end in itself, with each system of transportation trying to cut the throat of the other, it is time we began to think in terms of co-operation in respect to our transportation system.
In common, no doubt, with most other hon. members, I have had representations from trucking concerns and motor transport companies complaining bitterly about the encroachment of the railways upon their type of business. Plenty of evidence can be obtained from the railroads taking the opposite view. I think we in this country can make ourselves almost ridiculous if we go too far in that direction, if we take it that competition is such a good thing that we must compete each other to death. Even the most rabid private enterpriser, I think, will admit that when it comes to certain public utilities-and transportation is fast becoming a public utility in this country-there is a field for public ownership, or at least for a certain amount of social control in order that we may have co-ordination and synchronization of transport for the convenience and use of the public. I believe the criterion should be efficiency, convenience, and value for dollars spent, rather than the financial or commercial success of any form of transportation.
I will conclude, Mr. Speaker, by making a further plea to the government to consider carefully the question of acceding to the reasonable request made from this side of the house that a stay of the imposition of these freight rates be granted until the provinces have had an opportunity to prepare and submit their case in the proper way to the proper body.

maintopic: FREIGHT RATES-INCREASES ORDERED BY TRANSPORT BOARD-AMENDMENT, MR. COLDWELL- SUBAMENDMENT, MR. BRACKEN
speechtext:
I should like to offer a few comments, Mr. Speaker, on this freight rate issue. First of all I should like to quote the order in council under date of April 7, P.C. 1486:
The committee of the privy council have had before them the petition of the transportation commission of the maritime board of trade (representing, inter alia, the governments of the provinces of Nova Scotia. New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island), and representations on behalf of the governments of the provinces of Manitoba, Saskatchewan, Alberta and British Columbia to vary order No. 70425 of the board of transport commissioners for Canada of March 30, 1948, by providing that tariff schedules published and filed under the provisions of the said order be not effective until at least thirty days from the date of the said order.
The committee of the privy council, having given due consideration to the said petitions and representations, are unable to advise that the said order of the board of transport commissioners for Canada be varied in the sense requested.
This was signed by A. D. P. Heeney, clerk of the privy council.
As a further basis for my remarks I should like to quote the amendment which was so
Freight Rates

well introduced by my leader (Mr. Bracken), and also to endorse all the arguments so well advanced by him in presenting that amendment on April 13 with regard to this issue. The amendment reads:
That all the words after "this house" in the fourth line of the amendment be deleted, and that the following be substituted instead thereof:
"regrets the government's failure to secure the removal of inequalities and discriminations in the Canadian railway freight rates structure before the imposition of a horizontal increase of twenty-one per cent-an increase which is bound to intensify the aforesaid inequalities and discriminations; and
"Furthermore regrets that the government has refused the reasonable request of seven provinces that the imposition of increased freight rates recently authorized by the board of transport commissioners be delayed for thirty days until they could be heard."
The granting of this increase by the board certainly is going to intensify these discriminations, and in many cases will result in hardship upon those least able to pay. To some of these small shippers the increase will be as much as fifty per cent; to those who cannot afford to buy large quantities the burden will be great.
The situation is worse west of Fort William, where we find the mileage principle introduced. For instance, in parts of the prairie provinces we have to pay $169 more for a Chrysler car produced in Windsor than you pay for it in Ontario. For a light delivery truck we pay $150 more per unit than in Ontario. On an electric range we pay approximately $7 more, while the difference on refrigerators runs anywhere from $6.25 to $12.75 more per unit. For an ordinary washing machine we pay approximately $5 more per unit on the prairies than you do in the east. The farmer certainly is penalized, because he pays approximately $48 more for his binder than is charged in Ontario, -while on the 16 to 25 horsepower tractor the difference is $112.
I might go on and quote many other items, but perhaps a few figures as to freight charges for comparable distances would be sufficient. On an average haul of one hundred miles there is a difference of 4-6 per cent. On a haul of four hundred m-iles the rate is 12 per cent higher on the prairies than in the east. On grain we pay 13 per cent more per ton mile, and on lumber, which is quite an item to many producer's on the prairies, the difference is 31T per cent more per ton mile. On some commodities the difference is much greater. In certain parts of Alberta it is as much as 85 per cent more than in Ontario for certain distances. On bituminous coal the difference is 36-6 per cent.

I spoke of the difference on lumber. I would remind this house that according to the last issue of the Bank of Canada statistical summary the price of lumber in this country has advanced more than 216 per cent, and that does not take into account the higher freight rates, which will be a further increase. That is going to be quite an item for many people throughout the prairies. Certainly it will add to the cost of living. According to that same statement the cost of living index for the previous month was 150-8, an all-time high in the history of Canada; and again that did not take into consideration these increased freight rates. The other day the Minister of Transport (Mr. Chevrier), while presenting his argument in defence of the increase, placed on Hansard at page 2903 a table showing the rates from sources of supply to certain points in Canada. According to this table the greatest increase in the freight rate on lumber is on shipments to Manitoba, that increase ranging from $1.86-7 to $3.85-3 per thousand feet.
I have listened to arguments presented in behalf of various parts of Canada, the mari-times, British Columbia and so on. While I agree that the situation is difficult in British Columbia, I should like to place on Hansard certain figures which will give some idea of the benefit derived from competitive water rates. These figures deal with the year 1945, but I do not think there has been any significant change since that time.
The rate from Montreal to Vancouver on calcium phosphate is 75 cents, while the rate from Montreal to Calgary, because of the mountain differential, is $2,344. On ammonia the rate from Montreal to Vancouver is $1.25; to Calgary it is $2,334. On glassware the rate to Vancouver is $1.34 and $1.98 to Calgary. The rate on window glass is $1.00 to Vancouver and $1.98 to Calgary. On paint and varnish the rate is $1.25 to Vancouver and $1.98 to Calgary. The rate on barbed wire is 75 cents to Vancouver and $1.98 to Calgary, while on hardware and tools the respective rates are $1.25 and $1.98. I could mention such other items as structural steel, iron pipe, canned goods, and so on, but I do not think it necessary at this time.
As I say, those differences result from the zoning and the mountain differential, and I am afraid many people in Canada do not realize that these materials can be shipped much greater distances at considerable saving when they are sent by water. In any event, the people of Alberta probably bear the greatest brunt of these discriminatory freight rates; and this further increase is certain to add to their burdens.

Freight Rates
I certainly believe something should be done to equalize freight rates in this country, thoqgh I am not sure how that might be brought about. In the Globe and Mail of this morning I noticed an editorial dealing with this matter, headed, "The answer is more people". The editorial says:
The immediate issue before the house was whether railway freight rates should be advanced by 2il per cent in accordance with the ruling of the transport commission. The government is in favour of granting the increase at once. Objectors argue that, to begin with, certain "discriminations" should be ironed out. This demand, of course, comes exclusively from the western and maritime provinces, which, as everyone admits, will have to carry the large burden of the higher railway charges.
Further on the editorial continues:
Why must the people of the west and the maritimes rescue the railways by paying higher freight rates while Ontario and Quebec escape the extra levy almost entirely? It looks unfair, but it is not due either to the w-icked selfishness of the central provinces or to special privileges they enjoy. The reason for it is^ that they are in a competitively favourable position. Ontario and Quebec are, by Canadian standards, well populated and originate much traffic. Furthermore, it is traffic which can move by water or highway if railway charges go too high. Therefore freight rates are lower here than in parts of the country which are thinly populated and lack the services of ships and trucks. This is inescapable economics which no amount of argument can alter.
Further on the editorial states:
It takes very little imagination to see that the right answer "to the freight rates problem-the way to make transport cheap for the people of the now unfavoured regions-is to increase their numbers by immigration.
Then the last sentence reads:
What the country needs is a bold conception of its own future and some practical leadership.
Well, Mr. Speaker, I wish the problem were as simple as that. I agree with those comments; I hold no brief either for or against these two great provinces of Ontario and Quebec. But I do not believe immigration will take care of this problem in Canada. I want to put myself on record as to this question of immigration. More than once in this house I have argued for a much greater selective immigration to this country; but that would not cure the present difficulty. I have before me The Economic Annalist, issued by the federal Department of Agriculture. On page 5 it is pointed out that in 1946 there were 59,000 fewer people living on the prairies than in 1941. Most of the decline took place in Saskatchewan, but this movement is felt in the three western provinces, and it has been continuing since those figures, the latest available, were issued. In the same article I find this statement:
The number of people living on farms in Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta declined by about 145,000, or nearly 13 per cent, in the period between 1941 and 1946.
My point is that under the policies of this government, both during the war years and today, that movement has been taking place; and it would be unfair and unjust to attempt to cure it by immigration without at the same time altering those governmental policies which have been responsible for it.
The following statement was made by the United States agricultural attache at Ottawa, Mr. Francis A. Flood, when he addressed the federation of agriculture at Brockville this past winter. I quote just one paragraph of his speech, a report of which appeared in the Rural Co-operator, as follows:
I have heard Doctor J. F. Booth, of your Department of Agriculture, say that Manitoba and North Dakota have more in common with each other than Manitoba and Ontario or than North Dakota and New York state; that New York state and Ontario have more in common, with each other than they do with their own prairie states.
The lines of similarity seem to run north and south rather than east and west-so that had arbitrary political lines been run north and south instead of east and west like the Mason-Dixon line and the border here, there would really have been more sense to it from the economic and social standpoint.
I want to make my position clear. I have always been proud of this Canadian nation. I have never had any time for those who talk about seceding or anything of that nature. However, I do want to point out the difficulties and strains faced by our confederation. I have pointed out repeatedly that I do not think we are making the most of our great nation. We have probably more undeveloped resources than any other country. We have many sparsely populated areas, and with the proper policy we could easily make a much greater nation of Canada than has been done during the past.
Further to the contrast between conditions in North Dakota and Manitoba-the province with which I am best acquainted, although I do considerable travelling in North Dakota- I have before me 'a recent issue of Searle's grain index, which gives a comparison of the cash receipts of the United States farmer and the Canadian prairie farmer. It shows that the cash receipts of the prairie farmer in 1947 for all farm products averaged $3,623 per farm family, while the cash receipts in the state of North Dakota averaged $14,940 per farm family. That is gross income, but I would

think the percentages would be the same for net income. This gives some idea of the economic trials during the past years of the farmer on the prairies as compared with the farmer in the United States.
I have another editorial here to which I should like to refer; it was published in a journal which certainly cannot be accused of being anti-Liberal-the Winnipeg Free Press. The issue of April 12 contains an editorial headed, "A blow at the west." It is a long editorial and I shall read only portions of it. I quote:
Thus the burden of the $70 million per year increase now granted to the railways must fall chiefly upon the west and to a lesser extent upon the maritimes.
Having decided to oppose the board's judgment, the seven provincial governments did two things: they asked the dominion government by telegraph to postpone the coming into effect of the rate increase until after their appeal has been heard, and seeond, they agreed to meet at Ottawa on April 24 to work out a common procedure of appeal.
So matters rested until Wednesday, last, when Hon. Lionel Chevrier, dominion Minister of Transport, stated in the House of Commons that although petitions of appeal had been received from the seven provincial governments, the dominion government "has decided that it should not interfere with the effective date of the board's order." He qualified this statement with the phrase "without prejudice to any appeal." At the same time he tabled a copy of order in council (P.C. 1486) passed on April 7. This order states that the cabinet has before it the petitions of Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, Prince Edward Island, and the representations of Manitoba, Saskatchewan, Alberta and British Columbia and proceeds:
"The committee of the privy council, having given due consideration to the said petitions and representations, are unable to advise that the said order of the board of transport commissioners for Canada be varied in the sense requested."
Not since the transport board, a quarter century ago, undertook to throw out Crowsnest Pass rates has western Canada been treated so rudely and harshly . . .

speechtext:
Without quoting it I would say that the editorial goes on to- point out that the minister's statement did not appear in the order in council. The editorial says that it is a misstatement of fact, and it goes on to say that as the government has handled these seven provinces very shabbily, surely the members from British Columbia and the prairie and maritime provinces will represent the people who sent them to the house as members of parliament.
In contrast to the editorial in that great Liberal journal, which certainly was written with great feeling, it has been a surprise to me during the last few days that supporters of the government from British Columbia, the prairies and the maritimes should rise in their places in this house and ignore completely the wishes of the vast majority of the people who had made it possible for them to be members of this House of Commons. More than that, they have completely ignored these requests from the governments of the provinces from which they come.
During the time that I have been privileged to be a member here I have given careful study to this matter, and have come to the conclusion that I should vote and talk in the interests, first of the people in my riding, then of the people in the great province from which I come, and then of the people of Canada generally. I would hope that every member of this House of Commons would so vote on this important issue of freight rates.
I remember that in the past a great issue was made of an incident when the Prime Minister, probably in some heat-I was not a member at that time-said that he would not give a five-cent piece to a Conservative government in any province. What is the situation today? First of all we have a coalition government in British Columbia. Then in Alberta there is a Social -Credit government. In Saskatchewan there is a CjC.F. government. In the great middle province of Manitoba we have a very efficient coalition government.

There is one standing right here who will vote as his conscience dictates. Then we go to New Brunswick, where they have a Liberal government. There are the provinces of Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Island where they have their Liberal

governments. Therefore it is difficult for me * to understand the attitude of the Minister of Transport, the Prime Minister, and this government.
They may think that they are showing a strong hand, but I think it is really a sign of decay, a case of being in office too long. They might well have heeded the request of these seven provincial governments and stayed this judgment for some thirty days while the arguments of the provinces were being prepared, so that they could discuss the matter with the department and the government on a proper basis.

I should be happy if I could ever rival the Minister of Transport in political astuteness.
I do not wish to take up more time, Mr. Speaker. In conclusion I earnestly appeal to every member of this house to give thought to the welfare of the people who sent him here. According to the Ottawa Journal this government had a very serious caucus of its members last Tuesday, and it is reported that the Prime Minister told them that this parliament should live out its full term. He probably threatened some of the boys with an election, which would not be palatable to many of them if the issue were increased freight rates. It has been amusing to me to see some of the boys opposite who were regarded almost as outlaws a few days ago now coming back into the house and attempting to swallow themselves on this great issue. I trust that every member of the house, irrespective of political affiliation, will vote in the interests of the constituents who sent them here and bear in mind the request which has been made by seven provincial premiers for a stay of the board's order.

maintopic: FREIGHT RATES-INCREASES ORDERED BY TRANSPORT BOARD-AMENDMENT, MR. COLDWELL- SUBAMENDMENT, MR. BRACKEN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, many members have spoken eloquently in this debate, but a good deal of material is still available that has not been discussed, and I propose to introduce some new ideas.
In the first place I would urge upon the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) that he stay in Ottawa a little more. I realize that pressing duties take him away from the capital from time to time, but it is unfortunate that in two major catastrophes occurring within the last six months the minister was away from Ottawa. I refer to the government's policy in connection with coarse grains which was announced last fall when the minister was in Saskatchewan, and to the recent decision of the board of transport commissioners increasing freight rates. I feel that the minister's absence places him in a very embarrassing position when he has to go back and justify government policy to his friends in Saskatchewan.
In view of the fact that seven of the nine provincial premiers are slated to be in Ottawa this month to interview the government, I cannot think of any good reason why the operation of the board's order could not have been stayed until the premiers were given the opportunity to speak for the people they represent.
I also cannot understand why the government has not taken action to give some relief to the Canadian National Railways in its overcapitalization. This is a problem which has been on our hands for many years, and if the government was really concerned about its own railway it could have afforded relief by adjusting the railway's capitalization. Prior to the amalgamation of the different railways into the Canadian National Railways system these railways were running in the red at the rate of nearly $1,000,000 a week, and I think it was quite unreasonable to ask the publicly-owned utility to take over a bankrupt set of railways and try to operate them in the clear year after year.
When the president of the Canadian National Railways, Mr. Vaughan, was before the railways and shipping committee in 1946 he outlined in some detail the proposals which his company had made to the government. At page 19 of the evidence he said:
I referred last year to a recommendation of mine that the government accept income bonds of the Canadian National Railway Company in payment of the amount owing by the railway to the government for repatriation of British * securities.
Mr. Vaughan also presented a table to the committee comparing the position of the Canadian National Railways with first-class
Freight Rates

railways in the United States. It showed that the Canadian National Railways had a ratio of fixed charges to operating revenues in 1939 of 26-24 per cent. Its competitor in Canada, the Canadian Pacific Railway, had a ratio of 16-76 per cent; the Pennsylvania Railway, 18-47 per cent; the New York Central, 14-10 per cent; the Southern Pacific, 13-79 per cent; the Atchison, Topeka and Santa Fe, 6-91 percent; the Union Pacific, 8-66 per cent; the Baltimore and Ohio, 12-68 per cent. The class one railways of the United States which I have just mentioned averaged a ratio of 15-21 per cent. By 1944, owing to accelerated .var traffic, there was a marked improvement in the ratio of all these companies, but still the Canadian National Railways was forced to operate at a very serious disadvantage. Its ratio had been reduced to 11-44 as compared with 6-50 for the Canadian Pacific, and 6-00 for the class one railroads which I have just mentioned in the United States.
At page 25 Mr. Vaughan said:
If the government of the day had not wished or desired to protect private capital, a number of the railways which now make up the Canadian National would have been forced into liquidation because of the fact that they could not meet the interest charges on their funded debt, and the result would have been that their funded debt would have been reduced to a point where they could earn interest charges on it.

I am not suggesting that the Canadian government should have asked people outside of Canada who had invested their money in the Canadian National Railways securities to take a loss on their investment. What I am saying is that the government should place the financial balance sheet of the Canadian National Railways in a proper light so that the railway would not for ever be held up to the criticism of those who oppose public ownership that it is always running in the red.
The president of the railway was asked by the hon. member for Rosedale (Mr. Jackman) whether the railway would be satisfied if the proposals made by the president the year

before, that the government accept income bonds in payment of amounts owing by the railway, were accepted. Mr. Vaughan replied:
We would say that we should have a proper set-up, one which would make our fixed charges not more than twenty-five per cent of what they are today. If you do that, if you would make our fixed charges not more than 25 per cent of what they are, we would not come back again. But this would be only a partial remedy of the situation.
I might say that on the basis of the financial statement we had before us at that time, that sort of adjustment would have given the Canadian National Railways around $30,000,000 a year more than they had.

speechtext: I was interested in reading some of the evidence given by the late Senator McGeer at the hearings in Vancouver in June of last year. I understand that the late Senator McGeer spoke for nearly four hours during the hearings, and made such an eloquent argument that none of the counsel appearing for the railways was able to pick any flaws in his case or embarrass him in any detail. Senator McGeer made reference to the very large percentage of preference holdings outside of Canada. In looking up the annual report for this year I was interested to find on page 20 that -51 of one per cent of the preference holdings were held in Canada, 96-64 per cent in the United Kingdom, -34 of one per cent in the United States, and 2-51 per cent in other countries.

The Canadian Pacific. The late Senator McGeer was very eloquent in protesting against a proposal to increase the toll on Canadian citizens to protect such a large number of people living outside of Canada. He had something to say about the board of directors; he said that there is only one member of the board of directors who lives west of Toronto, the Hon. Eric W. Hamber, Vancouver. He pointed out that the list of directors includes: The Right Hon. Sir John Anderson, London, England; Edwin G. Baker, Toronto; L. J. Belnap, Montreal; Hon. F. Philippe Brais, Montreal; D'Alton C. Coleman, Montreal; Hon. Charles A. Dunning, Montreal; G. Blair Gordon, Montreal; Hon. Eric W. Hamber, Vancouver; John W. Hobbs, Toronto; Louis, L. Lang, Kitchener; W. A. Mather, Montreal; R. S. McLaughlin, Oshawa; Ross H. McMaster Montreal; Sir Edward Peacock, London, England; Howard P. Robinson, Saint John; Robert C. Stanley, New York; G. A. Walker, ICC., Montreal. Senator McGeer had some rather unkind remarks to make about his old friend, Hon. Charles Dunning. He said:
Take Hon. Charles Dunning. He started in England -and got everything in the way of progress from the confidence that western Canadians placed in him. Probably no one is more guilty in the estimation of railway men of making greater blunders in railway building in Canada than this same Mr. Charles Dunning.
On page 8332 of the evidence Senator McGeer referred to the 1946 Canadian National deficit of 88,961,000 resulting from including a charge for interest on government loans of $21,322,583. He said:
Why does the government of Canada want interest on its own public utilities? We financed this war through the chartered banks in substantial measure by using deposit certificates. We got the money at three-quarters of one per cent and every chartered bank financing the war on that basis was in the excess profits taxes brackets. Imagine a nationally-owned public utility corporation asking for an increase in rates to pay $21,00-0,090 of interest into the federal treasury, when in the post war period we lent England a billion -and) a quarter dollars for five years. We did not say to her that we wanted any interest. No, we said for five years you are to pay no interest. I am quite satisfied this case is not going to end here, no matter which way it is decided. Furthermore, I believe it must be dealt with as a matter of public policy, because I do not think that these railways or this board have any power to attempt to solve the situation by this proposed increase of rates. On the contrary, I am firmly of the opinion that it will require a national policy vigorously and effectively enforced, and in the formation of that national policy in our system of constitutional democracy, the high court is not the governor in council, it is public opinion.
I should like therefore to take this opportunity to urge hon. members, particularly on the government side, to take to heart the words of wisdom of the late Senator McGeer and to consider what is in the best interests of the people whom they represent. I might mention that excellent evidence was given by representatives from all the provinces, but I have made a special study of the evidence presented on behalf of Manitoba, Alberta and Saskatchewan. The government of Saskatchewan was in my opinion to be commended for having selected as chief counsel Hon. M. A. MacPherson, who was attorney general and provincial treasurer in a former Conservative administration. I believe that all who followed the hearings were convinced that Mr. MacPherson did an outstanding public service in cross-examining the witnesses and in presenting the case for the people, especially in the prairies.
On page 8 of the brief presented by the province of Saskatchewan it is pointed out that the effect of the increase would be inflationary, and that:
If these forces continue to hold up the current level of economic activity, then the proposed increase in freight rates could easily become a factor leading to a further inflationary rise in prices since it would lead in all probability to further demands for higher wages . . . The effect of the proposed increase in freight rates might easily be such as to bring a double impact upon the industrial areas of Canada.
Then on page 9:
Great as is the threat which a substantial increase in freight rates offers to the Canadian economy as a whole, a still greater danger lies in the extreme probability of further disruptions in regional and international relationships. In the first place, to the extent that prairie incomes over a term of years have tended to be lower than the national average, an increase in freight rates will be regressive in that the burden will be borne by those least able to support it. In the second place, as will be shown at length in other parts of this submission, the proposed increase would almost inevitably be reflected in further sharp reductions in western incomes.

Freight Rates
In the submission by the Edmonton chamber of commerce attention is drawn to the effect which the increase will have and what it will mean to the people in that province. The Alberta members have presented this case very well, but I was interested in the rates applying to flannelette blankets which move to Edmonton at a rate of $4.53, whereas the rate from Montreal to Vancouver is $1.75. I find that the citizens at Holden, which is 60 miles east of Edmonton, if they were interested in ascertaining the freight rates on this description of material shipped from Montreal, would receive some rather unusual advice from the agent. The agent would say to them, "If you are in a hurry for the material and want it shipped here directly we will give you one rate, but if you are not in a great hurry, if you are satisfied to have the material go from Montreal to Vancouver and shipped back from Vancouver to this town, 60 miles east of Edmonton, we will give you a rate of 21 cents per hundredweight less than that which you would be charged if the material were shipped here directly."
I submit therefore that it will be very difficult to convince the people in the prairies and in British Columbia that a further increase of 21 per cent in freight rates that are now out of line in those provinces should be imposed upon our people.
In the material prepared by the Saskatchewan government some time ago we have a comparison of freight rates between Megantic, Quebec, and Ingersoll, Ontario, 596 miles, where the rate on lumber is 24 cents. From Golden, British Columbia to Moose Jaw, the same distance, it is 40J cents. On lumber the western rates are 39 to 69 per cent higher than the eastern rates.
The cement rate from St. Mary's, Ontario, to Apple Hill, Ontario, 388 miles, is 22 cents, and from Winnipeg to Madrid, Saskatchewan, the same distance, 28 cents. The rates are 30 per cent higher.
On petroleum products the rates in the west are 35 per cent higher; on salt the rates are 30 per cent higher, and so all across the line. But there is no reason for that. It has been demonstrated by the railways that they can actually move material more economically in the wrest than they can in the rest of Canada. I have here the orders and regulations of the board of railway commissioners for September 1927, giving the actual cost of moving freight in the different provinces.

I was interested in the net earnings of the Canadian Pacific Railway over a period of years in the east and in the west respectively, during the depression years and the years of the war. Their net earnings were much higher in the west. These were the earnings in the east and in the west in the following years:

I think it is his opportunity now to perform an outstanding service to Canada and it is up to him to decide whether this injustice shall be perpetrated.
Speaking a few days ago, the hon. member commended the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) for the excellent speech he made. In fact he said it was the best speech the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar has delivered since 1940. I can assure the government that if some of my legal friends, the hon. member for Lake Centre or some other member of his profession, can show me how a motion can be introduced that will present this issue straight to the house, at least three British Columbia members will vote in favour of the motion, even it it should
Freight Rates

be a want of confidence motion, because we believe that the very future of our province is at stake in this matter.
The hon. member was right. The future of his province, as well as that of the prairie provinces, Nova Scotia, New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island, is at stake. Even if the government were defeated, if the members on the other side of the house are of the opinion that they have public opinion behind them, there would be no question of their coming back with a fresh mandate. But if the members of this house are not prepared now, as this debate closes, to stand up and be counted for or against this increase in freight rates, then we are going to introduce into our Canadian economic life a question that is so controversial that it will divide east and west more sharply than they have ever before been divided. It will make at least seven of the nine provinces feel that the dominion government has given them anything but a square deal.
We have heard from the hon. member for Vancouver North (Mr. Sinclair). He intimated that he was not one of the three mentioned by the hon. member for Fraser Valley. But we have not heard from the hon. member for Comox-Albemi (Mr. Gibson), the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Reid), or the hon. member for Fraser Valley (Mr. Cruick-shank) in this debate. I hope those three will make good the promise that was given a few days ago, to the effect that they are prepared to vote against this government and let the chips fall where they may.
Like the hon. member for Souris (Mr. Ross) who has just spoken, I have never had any time for those who advocated secession. Nothing would be gained by forming two or three separate countries within this dominion. Nothing would be gained by linking up with the United States. Within our democratic framework I think we have the machinery necessary to make it possible for us to iron out these differences.
I want to make my position clear. As far as the Canadian National Railways are concerned, I do not think the government needed to worry about giving them relief in this way at this particular time. I do not think the Canadian Pacific Railwaj' is in the position of needing help at this time. I feel it might have continued for at least another year until all the facts were thoroughly studied. I find that this railway has had generous treatment at the hands of the people. Again quoting from the board of railway commissioners for Canada, judgments, orders, regulations and rulings, under date of September 12, 1927, I find that the late Premier Oliver of

For the life of me I cannot understand why the government had to bring this increase into effect at once. Ever since I have been old enough, I have been borrowing from the banks, though perhaps my credit is not exceptionally good. To tell me that the two great railway companies could not have borrowed enough money to meet the demand for increased wages for only thirty days just does not make sense. I believe this action was an insult to seven premiers of Canada. I do not care what party they belong to; they represent seven of the provinces of Canada against the other two. All they asked was a delay of one month so that they could present

their case. As I say, I believe the government was wrong in not granting that thirty-day delay. maintopic: FREIGHT RATES-INCREASES ORDERED BY TRANSPORT BOARD-AMENDMENT, MR. COLDWELL- SUBAMENDMENT, MR. BRACKEN
speechtext: No.

maintopic: FREIGHT RATES-INCREASES ORDERED BY TRANSPORT BOARD-AMENDMENT, MR. COLDWELL- SUBAMENDMENT, MR. BRACKEN
speechtext: Perhaps not, except as to wages; but I say to the minister that if the railways of Canada will go bankrupt if they do not get that 21 per cent increase for thirty days, then it is time we took them both over and put in new management. What is most important to me in this connection, as I said the other day, is national unity. I do not believe you will ever get national unity in this country if two provinces can dictate to the other seven, and I do not care which two provinces they are. I am not referring to the members from either of those provinces who sit in this house. In my experience at Ottawa the members most willing to co-operate in anything which is in the best interests of Canada, particularly in the economic field, have been the members from the province of Quebec. I only wish the members from Ontario were the same. But I do not think any seven provinces should be imposed upon by the actions of the other two. I believe the government are mistaken in this policy, and in my opinion we shall get no action toward eliminating these discriminations for a long, long time if we depend upon the board of transport commissioners, without a directive from the government. The province of British Columbia has spent hundreds of thousands of dollars for the best legal talent it could engage.

maintopic: FREIGHT RATES-INCREASES ORDERED BY TRANSPORT BOARD-AMENDMENT, MR. COLDWELL- SUBAMENDMENT, MR. BRACKEN

maintopic: FREIGHT RATES-INCREASES ORDERED BY TRANSPORT BOARD-AMENDMENT, MR. COLDWELL- SUBAMENDMENT, MR. BRACKEN

That is quite true; the lawyers got enough to make up the deficit of the province of British Columbia. We shall now have to start all over again. According to the minister, the board has the authority to wipe out these differentials. In that case I think it is the duty of the board and the government to do so, without any further hearing. They have all the information already with respect to the mountain differential and other inequalities in certain parts of Canada. No one can tell me that the evidence presented to the transport commission by the greatest authority on freight rates we ever had in Canada, the late Senator McGeer, is not still on record; and there has been no great change in the meantime. Conditions may have

changed, but that has nothing to do with these inequalities; that is covered by the increase of 21 per cent. All the evidence with respect to the mountain differential is before the board, and I think it is the duty of the government to issue am absolute directive to that board. I do not see any point in setting up a royal commission or other special body, for if there is to be an inquiry they will have the same experts to advise them. I particularly object to the fact that the delay of thirty days was not granted in order to permit the seven premiers to appear before the cabinet.
I now wish to say a word with respect to the amendment moved by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bracken), which, at least in one respect, goes to the core of the matter, in that it describes the discrimination which is being practised as against certain parts of the country. I have not a copy of the subamendment before me, but if I remember correctly it suggests that before any increase was granted these discriminations should have been wiped out. With that I entirely agree. I am sorry I cannot support the C.C.F. amendment, because I do not think it means anything.

I think the members of the C.C.F. party will admit that they could not form a government, and even the junior Conservative party in the far corner will admit that with the material available at present, there would be little chance for the party across the way to form a government. So obviously if the amendment carried there would have to be a general election immediately. I think the C.C.F. are quite right in fighting against discriminatory freight rates, but I say they should force the issue on freight rates, but not on a straight motion of want of confidence, in the only party that can carry on under present conditions.

Today we have seven provinces which genuinely feel they have been sinned against and that, whether or not it is the fault of the provinces of Ontario and Quebec, somehow we are getting an advantage we should not have. I believe we in Ontario and Quebec are very much like the people of the rest of Canada. I do not think we want any unfair advantage. It is because the government, by its neglect, has allowed this situation to develop that I feel justified in voting, as I intend to vote, for the motion of want of confidence in the government.
I want to digress just for a moment on the question of freight rates, to make my position quite clear. I agree with what has been said, and said very well, by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) on another occasion. I agree that the railways must receive sufficient earnings to keep them sound. I agree with the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar that it is a discouraging and even demoralizing thing for the officials of the Canadian National Railways, and I mention them particularly, to travel along with deficits such as they now have. They had a deficit in 1947, a year of record high business. Therefore I say not only is that prima facie evidence, but it is obvious that the railways have to have additional earnings. How can anyone expect the railways, in the face of the terrific increase in costs during these last years, not to need an increase in their earnings?
I wish to make another point which is perhaps incidental. There is an idea that some way or another all deficits of the Canadian National Railways can be cured just by relieving it of a lot more of its indebtedness. There is no warrant for that belief. The Canadian National Railways has had many hundreds of millions of dollars of its indebtedness absorbed, and in my opinion rightly so, by the government of this country. That has been done because they were forced to take over and put together a number of lines that were not intended originally to be put together. Nevertheless the Canadian National now have an indebtedness to the public of only something less than 25 per cent of their apparent assets. They have an indebtedness to the public of, I think, only 5849-190J
some $582 million against apparent assets of well over $2,000 million. Therefore I say that this increase in rates is something which the railways needed.
I now come back to the main point. I think it is a lamentable thing, something which should not be tolerated, that we should have in Canada-goodness knows we have enough difficulties in this country, enough things to divide us-a further division of the country on this question of freight rates.
The other day the minister made a most excellent speech. I tell him that if ever I am in trouble and have a weak case and need counsel to defend me, I shall be glad indeed to be able to get his services. He made a most plausible and even persuasive argument that there was really no fault on the part of the government, that the fault was all on the part of the provinces. He told us, and I have no doubt he was correct in telling us, that during the course of the rate investigation it had been pointed out that this was purely a matter of rates and that everyone had agreed that it was no occasion on which to discuss discriminations. The minister pointed out further, and at the time I was quite impressed, that in a great many years there had been no appeals from the provinces, that, although they could have come in and appealed against these discriminations, they had not done so.

maintopic: FREIGHT RATES-INCREASES ORDERED BY TRANSPORT BOARD-AMENDMENT, MR. COLDWELL- SUBAMENDMENT, MR. BRACKEN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in the few remarks I have to make I believe I shall be introducing something new in this debate, and I am pleased to see the hon. member for Danforth (Mr. Harris) and other Ontario members now in their seats.
During this debate thus far we have heard little criticism regarding the necessity of increasing freight rates. It would appear as though the great majority of members who have taken part in this debate are convinced that an increase in freight rates is essential. The criticism that has been made is of the inequality of the way in which the rates are increased. I believe that, because of the increase in compensation paid to the railway employees and the enormously increased costs of materials used in the operation of the railroads, more revenue must be found, and sufficient evidence has been adduced to prove that this increase is necessary.
The chief criticism is that eastern Canada and western Canada must bear the greater part of the burden, while Ontario and Qudbec have little reason to complain. In other words, the failure to equalize the rates is responsible for the criticism levelled at the board of transport commissioners and the Department of Transport.
The increase was opposed by seven of the nine provinces. The neutral attitude taken by Ontario and Quebec would indicate that these provinces were not adversly affected.
If we wish to achieve the utopia of a united Canada, which appears to be approaching very slowly, sectionalism, the predominant factor in this debate, must be discarded, this atmosphere of suspicion completely cleared and a spirit of co-operation introduced in which we may approach this problem not as maritimers or as British Columbians, western or central Canadians, but as united Canadians.
I will take a few minutes to point out one of many circumstances in New Brunswick in which the citizens affected have developed a feeling of distrust toward industrialized central Canada. For many years in the town of St. Stephen, in the county I have the honour to represent, the St. Croix Soap Company manufactured an article used practically exclusively in the maritime provinces, and well known in
many other parts of Canada. Many citizens of this town were employed in this thriving industry. A few years ago Lever Bros., a large manufacturer in central Canada, approached the management of this small industry; they painted a glowing picture of the manner in which this little industry would grow if it were controlled by Lever Bros. The offer made to the owners, and the visions of a much larger industry, influenced the St. Croix Soap Company to sell their business to Lever Bros.
In a very short time production started to fall, and during the last war, when materials used in the manufacture of soap were in short supply, they were earmarked for central Canada. Eventually the manufacturing ceased in St. Stephen, and this small business, which means a lot to a small town, was moved to central Canada. We have left there at the present time an empty plant, and many of our citizens are out of employment.
The Mann Axe Company, in this same town, received exactly the same treatment, as did many other small industries in our province. This has brought about, as I have just said, a feeling of suspicion when you mention central Canada to a maritimer. As was pointed out yesterday by the hon. member for Royal (Mr. Brooks), the few manufacturing industries in the maritime provinces which have survived have done so on their merits by producing quality; for example, Ganong Bros, and Moir's, manufacturers of candies; Stanfield's products; Hartt, boots and shoes; Palmer, boots and shoes; Connors Bros., canned fish, and many others who produce quality goods known right across Canada.
Many of these manufacturers have a policy of one price to all. In other words, their commodities may be purchased in Vancouver at exactly the same price that we pay in the maritime provinces.	.
The Maritime Freight Rates Act provides that westbound freight from the maritimes shall be at a rate 20 per cent lower than that prevailing for eastbound freight to the maritimes. The new rate in no way affects this 20 per cent lower rate from the maritimes.
It has been suggested by several hon. members that if the railway board undertakes an investigation into the rate structure in this country it will not be completed in less than a year and a half or two years.
My belief is that conditions now prevailing can be greatly improved in a very short time if those who are in a position to assist are prepared to meet the challenge. I do not refer to the railway board or to the government of this country but to the manufacturers in
Freight Rates

central Canada who are protected by tariffs which have always operated to the disadvantage of the maritime provinces. The lowering of the tariff is one way of bringing about equalization.
Another method of approach would be for the manufacturers themselves to have one price only for every section of this country. This could-be done without costing the manufacturers a single dollar.
