speechtext:
That would be much preferable to granting subsidies, and I assure the house that it would bring about a much better feeling between the east and the west and central Canada.
I wish to refer to the table which the Minister of Transport (Mr. Chevrier) put on Hansard and to quote a paragraph from his remarks when introducing it. He said at page 2902 of Hansard:
A Chevrolet car moving east from Walkerville or Oshawa to Quebec will have to bear an increase of $7.33; to Montreal, $5.33; to Halifax, $7.86; to Toronto, $2.40; -to Winnipeg, $17.48; to Regina, $23.39; to Calgary, $29.73; to Vancouver, $31.26.
Mr. GIBSON (Comox-Alberni); Shame!
Mr. STUART (Charlotte); That will be the additional freight when the 21 per cent increase goes into effect. When the increase in the eight cities mentioned has been averaged you will find that the average increase is $15.58; the low in Toronto area of $2.40; the high in Vancouver of $31.26. The manufacture of this vehicle is exclusively in Ontario. This province received full benefit of the thousands employed and of the enormous -taxes paid by these large corporations which are protected by high tariffs.
No branch of this industry is established in the maritime provinces. We could purchase our cars in the same country in which we find markets for our produce were it not for tariff protection. Surely we are not taking a selfish attitude when a request is made to equalize the price of manufactured articles purchased from industrialized central Canada.
Many Ontario and Quebec manufacturers have already adopted this plan. For example, Tip Top Tailors, and many others, [DOT]have one price to all. I shall mention several that I believe should fall in line. To head the list would be manufacturers of cars and trucks, manufacturers of farm machinery and manufacturers of household appliances-

these appear on the list in Hansard-such as bathtubs, furnaces, stoves, refrigerators and hundreds of other household articles.
Another important item would be canned vegetables. Canned fish of all kinds, which are manufactured in the county I represent, are sold right across Canada at one price to all. They can be purchased in the city of Vancouver at the same price at which I can purchase them in the town in which I live. British Columbia salmon is another article that should sell in the maritime provinces for the same price at which it sells in British Columbia, and all vegetables that are canned in Ontario should have one price tag from Vancouver to Halifax.
Take, for example, manufacturers of cars and trucks. If they wish to adopt the idea that I have endeavoured to put forward they would have a record of the number of units delivered to each dealer in every part of Canada for several years. It would be a simple matter to find the average freight that should be charged right across the board. In this way those protected by tariffs-which is to the maritimer, as I have stated before, a subsidy-that benefit the citizens of central Canada only, would pay their proportional part in delivering the vehicle to the purchaser in eastern or western Canada.
Interprovincial trade, as well as international trade, must be a two-way street if it is to function successfully. Co-operation is essential. If the suggestions I have made should be adopted by manufacturers of central Canada, it would go a long way toward equalizing and balancing the freight rates that are under discussion at the present time. If hon. members from Ontario and Quebec are sincere in their desire to be helpful in this particular case, in no way could their sincerity be better exemplified than by pointing out to the manufacturers in their respective constituencies the unfair advantage they have taken of the citizens of eastern and western Canada, and at the same time use their influence in support of the removal of this gross injustice. This is not a problem for the government, but for the manufacturers themselves.
As I stated before, I am firmly convinced that an increase in freight rates was necessary; the burden, however, should not be borne by one or two provinces; it should be borne by all. This equalization can be realized to a great extent if we work, not

Freight Rates
as individuals for particular sections, but collectively as Canadians, and in doing so our united efforts would produce the desired result.

maintopic: FREIGHT RATES-INCREASES ORDERED BY TRANSPORT BOARD-AMENDMENT, MR. COLDWELL- SUBAMENDMENT, MR. BRACKEN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in rising at this stage of a long and very fine debate I propose to make several brief observations on a question which is so vital to the maritime provinces generally and particularly to the constituency of Halifax. I propose to vote against the amendment moved by the leader of the C.C.F. party (Mr. Coldwell) and the amendment to the amendment of the leader of the official opposition (Mr. Bracken). I can summarize briefly my reasons for voting as I intend to do.
However, before I develop the one or two points with which I wish to deal I should like to refer briefly to the matter brought up earlier in the debate this afternoon by the hon. member for Dauphin (Mr. Zaplitny). He referred to a press report originating in Halifax relating to a situation in respect of which I had already received representations. I have been able to secure certain information relating to this matter which I should like to put on Hansard in order that the hon. member for Dauphin may realize the situation to which the newspaper report refers.
The hon. member made reference to two ships which have been diverted from Halifax. The first is the English Prince. This ship cleared from England under orders to proceed to Halifax or Montreal, depending on the opening of the St. Lawrence river. As a result of the opening of the St. Lawrence river this ship, while on the Atlantic has apparently decided to proceed to Montreal. This decision had absolutely no reference to the 21 per cent increase in freight rates. I would point out to the hon. member for Dauphin that it is specifically provided in the order of the board that the 21 per cent increase is not to apply to import-export rates through Canadian ports.
The other ship to which reference was made is the Martha Kleppe. This ship had a cargo consisting, in part, of some 2,200 tons of peanuts destined to a firm in Hamilton. I am advised that negotiations for re-routing this ship were in progress before the decision of the board of transport commissioners was handed down, and the decision to re-route this cargo through New York has no reference at all to the board's decision. As a matter of fact, not one ton of cargo in either of these ships was affected by the 21 per cent increase in the freight rates.
The decision of the board of transport commissioners has been to authorize a horizontal
increase in the rates of ordinary freight within Canada. This increase is contrary to the representations so forcefully made by counsel for the maritime provinces who appeared at the hearing. It is contrary also to what is conceived to be the spirit and the principle of the Maritime Freight Rates Act and, perhaps most important of all, it is contrary to what many conceive to be the essential interests of the development and the healthy continuance of the economic situation in the maritime provinces.
Protests against this horizontal increase have been widespread throughout the maritimes and in other parts of .Canada and these protests have resulted in the announcement of the premiers of seven provinces of an appeal from this decision. The Minister of Transport (Mr. Chevrier) has clearly stated that the government is prepared to hear this appeal and to deal with it when it is made. I should like, as simply and as briefly as I can, to sum up the situation as I see it in its application to the maritime provinces.
As a result of the Duncan commission of
1926,	which was a wide and searching inquiry into the whole economic system of the maritime provinces, the Maritime Freight Rates Act was passed by the federal parliament in
1927.	The purpose and basis of this act were to equalize existing discriminations against the economy of the area of the three maritime provinces and to do away with certain disabilities which had been imposed upon the economic development of those provinces.
Both before and after that commission and the enactment of the Maritime Freight Rates Act, the board of transport commissioners in various decisions has considered the powers which are given to it under the Railway Act to deal with the question of discrimination and inequalities. It has also, not less importantly, made decisions with respect to the matters and considerations of which, under the act, it is permitted to take cognizance in determining applications of this kind.
My own view is that the board of transport commissioners, in the past, has taken the position that it is not empowered to deal with the kind of discrimination and the inequalities against which we complain in the maritime provinces and, further, that it is not empowered under the act to give consideration to the problems of geography and of distance which we say are the very considerations to which, most importantly, regard should be had in dealing with 'the difficulties under which we operate in the maritime provinces.
This view which I have stated is not shared unanimously. The government, by the order
Freight Rates

in council presented to the house by the Minister of Transport, has instructed the board of transport commissioners to institute a full and searching inquiry into the question of discrimination. The wording of the order in council is addressed to the board and instructs it to make an investigation with a view to establishing a fair and reasonable rate structure which will, under substantially similar circumstances and conditions, be equal in its application to all persons and localities in the various provinces and territories of'Canada.
This is in line with the suggestion made by my colleague the senior member for Halifax (Mr. Isnor) when speaking in this house on April 5. In stating to the house the basis on which the government had passed this order in council, the Minister of Transport, speaking earlier in the debate, clearly stated his opinion that the board has full powers to deal with all questions of discrimination and inequalities which may exist in the rate structure throughout the dominion, and in addition he has stated that the chairman of the board of transport commissioners has said to him that is also his view of the situation.
I submit that this must be understood as instructions from the government to the board, with respect to the investigation which they have authorized it to make, to exercise its full plenary powers, whatever powers it may have under the act, to carry out a full investigation and to reach a decision on the matter referred to it.
In my opinion this is exactly what is needed to settle the problem from the point of view of the maritime provinces. There is at present confusion as to the powers of the board and as to the division of responsibility for the freight rates structure as between the board of transport commissioners and the government.
When the board of transport commissioners has completed the investigation which it has now been instructed to undertake, and has rendered a decision, all the inequalities or discriminations which may exist should be out in the open and be a matter of record.
In rendering its decision, the board will have to do one of three things. It will have to deal with these discriminations and inequalities in a satisfactory manner; or, secondly, it will have to refuse to deal with them by reason of the fact that it finds it lacks the power to deal with them or that it is restricted, under the provisions of the Railway Act, in the considerations which it is permitted to explore and to take into account in dealing with these matters; or, thirdly, it will bring down a decision which will be found unsatisfactory to the interested provinces.

It is my hope that the board will deal with all the outstanding questions in a satisfactory manner. That would be the object of the inquiry.	But if that is not the case, the
reason or reasons whereby it has been unable to deal with these matters satisfactorily will be clear to all. It will then be possible to refer any outstanding questions to the government in the sure knowledge that there can be no question in anybody's mind as to where the responsibility lies and on whose authority proper decisions must be arrived at.
I am therefore supporting the government and refusing to support the amendment and the amendment to the amendment for two reasons. One is the expressed and evident desire of the government to consider any appeal which it may be thought proper to make against the present order of the board. The second is that the decision of the government to refer to the board a full and complete inquiry is the quickest and the best method of settling the question of discrimination and inequalities, and of disposing, in the best and the quickest possible way, of any outstanding questions of divided responsibility and jurisdiction with respect to the question of freight rates, which, as has already been said, is one of the most important and serious questions we have to face at the present time.

No. I can assure the minister that if ever again there is a shortage or a near shortage, he will be bombarded with more questions.
The question of freight rates is, without doubt, probably the most important question that has been brought before the house in some time. Perhaps anything I say on this occasion will be more or less a matter of repetition. However, there are a few things I wish to touch on that are vital in connection with the problems of Prince Edward Island.
In speaking on this question a few days ago, I said it was my opinion-and nothing has yet been produced to change that opinion-that the board of transport commissioners have no authority to set fixed rates for the railways when, as I see it, the authority to fix those rates rests entirely with the government of the day. But they were entitled to make suggestions to the government; and then it was for the government to decide. I do not think the commission has the authority of a court. In fact, while they can bring in submissions to the government, I do not think the government should lose sight of the fact that they have the right to say, right there and then, either that they accept or reject them.
In this case, however, the Minister of Transport, acting for the government, seemed to be in a great hurry to put these increases into effect immediately without due consideration being given to the provinces that were most affected. In my opinion it would have been a better policy had the Minister of Transport listened to the protests that were immediately raised by the seven provinces of Canada in regard to what they called discrimination in reference to them. On this point I might say that I believe the premiers of the seven 5849-191
provinces will be in attendance here in Ottawa in the course of a day or two, but in the meantime this question may be definitely decided. Whether the vote goes one way or the other, the question may be definitely decided and the premiers of the seven provinces will not then have a hearing that is worthwhile.
As I said in speaking about the Canadian National Railways a few days ago, that railway is government-owned and, during the last few months, submitted a statement to the government pointing out that it could not operate under present conditions and asking for a thirty per cent increase in freight rates. The board of transport commissioners, after reviewing the case, come along and say, "No. We can recommend to the government a horizontal increase in the freight rates right across Canada of only 21 per cent".
Perhaps if another investigation were made, the next report would look at the finances of the Canadian National Railways and Canadian Pacific Railway Company in a different light, and we might have only a ten per cent horizontal increase right across Canada. Therefore I think the government were in too much of a hurry in bringing this matter up for an immediate decision. I think the government should have done as the premiers of the seven provinces had urged upon them, namely, wait at least thirty days until some further consideration had been given to the matter.
In reference to the railways, before this matter was really brought into the open, when I was speaking on the speech from the throne I urged strongly on the railway department that certain things should be done with reference to railway men in each province. For instance, I urged that there should be an increase in the pensions given to railway men, especially those who were in the lower wage brackets. When the house took recess at six o'clock I was talking about the discrimination against our cash crop of potatoes. As hon. members are aware, this is a perishable crop as compared with wheat and it needs a great deal of care in storage and handling prior to shipment. I submit that the board should have given special consideration to our cash crop as has been given to the cash crop of wheat in the west.
When the Minister of Transport was making his able speech with reference to this subject a few nights ago he seemed to fear that if this measure did not carry as suggested by him there would be amalgamation of the two great railroads. I would remind him of the slogan that we used to hear at one time: "Amalgamation never, competition ever." We have no fear of amalgamation in Prince Edward Island because there is no competition as far as the railroads are concerned.
This is a serious question for our producers. For instance, our shippers were handicapped for a time last winter because of a shortage of reefer cars. If there is a shortage of cars in New Brunswick the people there can appeal to the Canadian Pacific and obtain the same number of cars that they would procure from the Canadian National. Since we have no competition, we are entirely in the hands of the government-owned Canadian National. I was glad to be able to put on the record that the Minister of Transport had been able to meet the need for reefer cars. However, as I said, if there were competition we could appeal to the Canadian Pacific when such a shortage arose.
The other night the hon. member for Royal stated that he had received a great many telegrams, letters and telephone calls from people in the maritimes. I think most hon. members from the maritime provinces have received scores of telegrams, letters and telephone messages demanding that the members from the maritimes stick together on this issue and fight to have it left as it was before, especially as far as the maritime provinces are concerned.
When the hon. member for Waterloo South (Mr. Homuth) was speaking on this question

Freight Rates
.the other night he said that in his opinion the great province of Ontario would be willing to pay its share of the cost of any revision of freight rates. I suppose it was quite reasonable for him to say that, because if there is a deficit to be paid by the government it would mean that Ontario, considering the amount of taxes which that province pays, would probably pay 50 to 60 per cent of the deficit.
While I can speak for only a few members from the maritime provinces, I know that they have received letters and telegrams from their own people, most of them complaining of a violation of the terms of confederation and the provisions of the freight rates act of 1927 as well as of the recommendations of the Duncan commission of 1926.
Apart from repeating what the hon. member for Royal has said, I have covered the ground pretty well. Prince Edward Island is differently situated from New Brunswick and Nova Scotia. Those provinces produce certain manufactured goods but there are few industrial plants in Prince Edward Island. Our province is largely agricultural. If this commission were making due inquiry into the conditions of our province with reference to the freight shipped therefrom I cannot understand why they should ask the government to nullify the provisions of the Maritime Freight Rates Act and the recommendations of the Duncan commission.
A demand has been made of most members from the maritime provinces that we implore the government through the Minister of Transport to delay this matter until the representatives of the seven provinces have had an opportunity to make their protests known to the government. I should like to read part of one telegram which I received, as follows:
We look to the members from the maritime provinces to fight for the restoration of our former position under the act.

maintopic: FREIGHT RATES-INCREASES ORDERED BY TRANSPORT BOARD-AMENDMENT, MR. COLDWELL- SUBAMENDMENT, MR. BRACKEN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, many excellent speeches have been delivered on the question of freight rates, and I feel thab I cannot add anything new, certainly not along the lines that have been covered so far. I am going to approach this subject from another angle and shall endeavour to make a suggestion or two. If they cannot be considered now, perhaps consideration will be given them later on.
I have in mind quite clearly what the minister said in his excellent speech. When the minister speaks he presents his arguments in a plain, matter of fact way so that everyone can understand what he means. I have in mind clearly what he said. Three facts stand out: No. 1, that we must have railways; No. 2,
that the railways must have more revenue, and No. 3, that there should be more freight.
I have asked myself, Mr. Speaker, just what are the reasons for the railway situation in Canada being what it is, and answering that to my own satisfaction, I then asked myself: Are we forever to be facing the problem of increasing freight rates every few years? Is there not some method by which we can have at least some fixity of railway tariffs?
I am not going to blame the railways in any shape or form, or anybody else, unless I blame all of us who are members. I remember quite a few years ago-I was not a member then-I had to come to Ottawa nearly every week, and I used to go and sit in the railway committee room where often in those days plans were placed before the members for railway extensions here, there, and everywhere throughout the country. Those were the days of railway expansion. Those who represented the railways had to contend against the members of parliament of those days who were pressing their demands for a railway in this direction or in that direction, and naturally they recommended that the railway run through their own community or somewhere near it. The members themselves were being besieged by everybody back home to see that the railway ran in their direction. As a result of all this pressure, the railways were compelled to build lines which their engineers told them, and which they knew themselves, were wholly uneconomic. That is one of the burdens with which our railways, have been afflicted down through the years and which has put them in the boat they are in today. I will give just four examples in different parts of the country.
If you were to travel away to the west, Your Honour, in the direction of the Alaska highway, you would have to pass through Edmonton if you went by rail. The railway after it leaves Edmonton has its terminus at Dawson Creek, but at the time the railway was built it was never determined that Dawson Creek should be the terminus. The railway hardly knew where it was to go. If had to meet the requests of members of parliament, who wanted it to go here and wanted it to go there, with the result that it, was constructed as far as McLennan Junction, about 267 miles north west of Edmonton. There it divided, and one branch went to the west on the north side of the Peace river to what is known as Hines Creek, where it ended up in the woods. It could not possibly bring results to the railway so far as traffic was concerned. The other part of the road
3002
Freight Rates

went on straight west from McLennan Junction. I do not believe at the time that the railway had any conception of where they were going to go, but they were being importuned by the members of parliament, and if I had been here I would likely have done the same as the members of those days did, supported the application for railway extensions into new parts of the country.
After McLennan junction you come in contact with a most peculiar situation. The railway, after a run of fifty miles, arrives at a place called Spirit River, and it ends there, ends nowhere, ends in the woods. When the road was projected toward Spirit River the intention was to proceed straight west, and the roadbed was built but not railed for another fifty miles toward a place called Pouce Coupe. But pressure was brought to bear on those building the road, and what happened? Today if you were travelling through that country, when you reached Spirit River you would find that the railway backs up five miles. It does not go forward; it does not even turn around; the whole train backs up to a place called Rycroft, because the pressure was excessive from the area now called Grande Prairie, a prosperous part of the country well worthy of a railway. At Rycroft the railway runs south for fifty miles, to an area quite foreign to where it had started for. Arriving at Grande Prairie, it runs northwest for approximately 100 miles to its present terminus at Dawson Creek. So every farmer and settler in that whole area is compelled to pay freight on an additional 100 miles and the railway is compelled to run its {rains that extra 100 miles to Dawson Creek. How can the railways pay under those conditions?
North of Dawson Creek is the only known area which can accommodate a great new immigration settlement, which has to come, for the railways must have more traffic, and the only way they can get it is by opening up the country. There is an area where perhaps 150,000 to 200,000 more farms are available for settlement. But unless something is done, the people who settle there will be compelled, for goodness knows how long, to pay freight on that extra 100 miles and travel that extra distance. I do not blame the railways for that, but it does add to their costs and reduces their profits. But they are not to blame for those conditions. It is we here who are to blame.
Having said that, I feel that any adjustment that is to be made to relieve the railways of these extra costs should be shared by the country at large, not just by the businessmen and merchants and people who are trying to carry on there.

Let me give another such example. Sup-, posing Your Honour is going to Flin Flon or to Sherridon, two great mining centres in a district that is opening up and growing very rapidly. It is on the pre-Cambrian shield, with much commerce by way of mining being conducted there. What happens? You take a train to Winnipeg and go away past Dauphin andi finally pass a place called Swan River. If you could only turn north from there it would be only 100 miles to The Pas, a fine city which is growing rapidly and destined to become great. It will be the centre of all that new mining area. But you cannot go straight north. You have to go away west to Hudson Bay junction. The railways had nothing to do with that. They were compelled to build that road which, like Topsy in Uncle Tom's Cabin, just "growed". Many of our railways just "growed up" without any relation to economics or traffic. That was not the fault of the railways. When you arrive at Hudson Bay junction you turn and go 100 miles northeast before you reach The Pas. In other words, you go another 100 miles out of your way.
So I am beginning to say to myself that the time has come for us to revamp the whole business associated with railways and give them a chance to live. They have not a chance under the conditions I have mentioned.
Suppose you were going to Arvida or Chicoutimi by rail, what would you have to do? First of all, you go west of Quebec city fifty miles. You go to a place called Riviere a Pierre. Then you turn to the north, and run 100 miles and come to Chambord. Then you turn to the right and run east fifty miles down to Jonquiere and Arvida and Chicoutimi. It is in the lower part of that part of Quebec, Jonquiere, Arvida and Chicoutimi, that the country is growing. It is a very great country, Your Honour, destined in my judgment to be a great industrial centre some day because of the cheap electricity that results from the vast plant at S'hipshaw and the vast waterpower resources which are behind it. Power can be developed there far cheaper than in any other place in the world. Therefore it is destined to become a great manufacturing country and a great agricultural country because up the Peribonka river, that country which was made famous by Louis Hemon in his book "Maria Chapdelaine" will be well settled. What does it mean? Until alterations are made there, it means that for all time the thousands and thousands of people who will settle in there will be compelled to go 100 miles out of their way because the railway just "growed up". It was not the fault of the railway. It was just extended to take in those areas.

Freight Rates
The hon. member for Cumberland (Mr. Black) was telling me yesterday-I have seen it myself; I knew something of it-that when the railway was being built on Cape Breton island there was a big debate in parliament on where they would run the railway from Mulgrave to Sydney. A great battle took place between those who wanted the railway to run in the centre of the island-I am not making any comment as to where it should have been run-or along the shore. It meant a distance of close to thirty-five or forty miles extra, via the centre route. Because of that, the fine city of Sydney, the coal mines and the steel plants there, have for years and years been compelled to ship their coal and steel forty miles farther than it was necessary for them to do. How can they compete against the world, as they have to do, when they have to go away out of their way? Not only that, but when you drive on the main line again you find that the railway is not where it should have been. It is not the fault of the railways. They were compelled to do things. Therefore, sir, I say that, not the maritime provinces, not the west, not Manitoba, but the whole of Canada must assume the burden of revamping the railways so that they will be in a position to carry freight at a lower rate.
I am not advocating the lower rate today. According to the board, the rates are too low. I accept the judgment of the board of transport commissioners. The minister said that one of two things would have to take place: either the railways would have to have a higher rate, or amalgamation of the two railways would have to take place. That has been advocated by some. I do not think it has ever been advocated by anyone who really understood the problem. Personally I could not support amalgamation of the railways. I am strongly in favour of the two railways. One is in opposition to the other, and each one meets the other and tries to do a better job.
If what the minister said is true we must choose one of two alternatives; either the rates must be higher, or we must accept amalgamation. Therefore it comes down to only one alternative, namely, higher rates. Having been in big business for many years, and having a keen conception of what freight rates mean to business, I say that increased freight rates at the present time would work a very great hardship on the maritime provinces-they are just trying to pull themselves together-and to British Columbia, also.
Therefore the problem is, what can we do? Something must be done. It is a problem to solve what can be done, because what the railways want is much more freight. If they had two or three times the amount of freight
they now have, even with the present rates, they would have a lot more revenue, perhaps enough to carry on. I do not know; it is not for me to say. But one thing is certain. They must have a lot more freight. They cannot get more freight by throttling business by higher rates in the maritime provinces. The maritime members have been saying what it would mean to their business to have higher freight rates, and I presume they are right. The British Columbia members in all parts of the house have said the same thing that increased freight rates would throttle their business which is struggling to go forward. I am inclined to agree with the members from the east and the west in that regard.
What can be done? That is the problem. We all admit that we must have the two railways. We all admit that the existing railways must have more revenue. There are only two ways in which they can get it, from an increased amount of freight or from higher freight rates. At the moment it is out of the question for them to get much more freight. I am going to submit a program which will result in much more freight, but it could not be worked out in a short time. Therefore I am going to suggest to the minister-it may be too late; I do not know whether it can be done now or not-to consider not putting into operation the new freight rates for some time. What would it matter if they were not put into operation for a year, provided that the government of this country, which I will support to do this, accept the deficits on each road resulting from the lack of the increased freight rates. That may not be possible. If that were acceptable- [DOT]

maintopic: FREIGHT RATES-INCREASES ORDERED BY TRANSPORT BOARD-AMENDMENT, MR. COLDWELL- SUBAMENDMENT, MR. BRACKEN
speechtext: It is possible, but it is a tremendous amount. It is against the policy of the government.

maintopic: FREIGHT RATES-INCREASES ORDERED BY TRANSPORT BOARD-AMENDMENT, MR. COLDWELL- SUBAMENDMENT, MR. BRACKEN
speechtext:
The minister is a bright young man, and I am sure he would like to give the suggestion some consideration. In any event, that is all I can say. I suggest that he abandon the increased rates on the condition that the country accept the deficit of these two roads. It is only fair that the country should do that until such time as the whole matter can be threshed out, which will be quite a problem. I know what the minister is up against. It will be quite a problem to face the premiers of the seven provinces.
Since I come from Ontario, I wish to put myself square with the country. As a citizen of Ontario I am willing to do whatever I possibly can to help both the east and the west, and that is the only way we can overcome the difficulty. Since I am an Ontario
Freight Rates

member and a taxpayer, I would be willing to pay my part; I am sure the people of Ontario would be willing to pay their part, and I would think the people of Quebec would be willing to pay part of the cost to provide for the deficits of the two roads until the whole matter could be studied again. I am as satisfied as I am standing here that the whole railway problem must be studied again. I do not think it is right that the railways should be compelled forever to be up against what they have been in the past, and make these endless journeys and endless additional costs without reason, to do business in parts of the country.
The minister may not agree with what I am now going to say. I am going to ask him to reconsider the building of a bridge over the strait of Canso. I was a member of the reconstruction committee two or three years ago. I heard engineers of both the roads, I believe-if it was not of both roads it was the engineers of the Canadian National Railways-tell the committee that a bridge across the strait of Canso would save the railroads a million dollars a year. If that is so-I am not going to say whether it is or not; the minister would know much better than I do, because he is in a position to know, with those who are behind him advising him who should know-then it is up to the government of Canada to build a bridge across the strait of Canso without cost to Nova Scotia, New Brunswick or the railways. -By this means the railways would get business and we would get the money all back again. The steel would all be made there and it would be a splendid thing for the city of Sydney to be able to produce that million tons of steel. A great deal of work would result in that part of the country, and heaven knows the people there need it. I offer that suggestion as one which in my opinion the minister should seriously consider.
I have made extensive surveys of bridges. I know there are half a dozen going up across the Mississippi; at St. Louis and at San Francisco they have constructed two gigantic bridges costing roughly $150 million each. That program has been carried out in the last few years, and there are now projected at San Francisco two more bridges at a cost of $200 million each. The people in the United States have done this because the bridges that have been built have proved to be wonderful dividend producers.
I suggest to the minister that he should not hesitate to put into effect a program which would enable the Canadian National

to carry out such an undertaking as I have described. It would be an investment that would return dividends, because certainly the building of a bridge across the strait of Canso would be one means whereby the yearly deficit could be cut down, to the extent of one million.
There is another suggestion I have to offer. I have been across the prairies many times, and it is my judgment that the western provinces have never had a square deal, nor have they had the chance of securing a square deal. It is not that they have not tried hard to get it. The railroads running through the prairies for perhaps a thousand miles pass through half a dozen communities, at most ten communities of any size producing freight. They carry wheat to the east, with very little freight going back, and the result is that the railway companies are faced with a colossal expenditure. This is not fair to these companies.
We must try to solve the problem that faces us in that respect. How are we to solve it? We should do the same for the west as for the maritimes-expand their industrial activities, both primary and secondary. So far as the west is concerned, I read only today that it may be ten years before the dam is constructed across the Saskatchewan river at Riverhurst or somewhere in that vicinity. If it were in my charge to build a dam across the Saskatchewan river, I would do it in a great deal less than ten years.
I have had a good deal to do with many dams, and in my judgment that is one thing which has to be done if we are to give the west a chance to produce freight. They are producing too little today in that part of Canada, not because of any inherent inability on their part. It is not their fault, because they cannot produce without water. The water is there simply flowdng into Hudson bay to make more ice.
If the increased rate of 21 per cent across the board were left off for some time, it would give the country an opportunity to get together and solve this gigantic railway problem, which must be solved in any event, because we cannot go on forever having an application every few years for increased freight rates. Let us have the problem settled once for all. I have suggested one or two ways in which it might be helped.
I do not want to take up much more time because I know the house is anxious to get the vote, but I have one or two more suggestions to offer the minister. He is a bright man, as I said to my deskmate yesterday. I should not like to say that he is the brightest on the government side but I spoke very highly of him to

Freight Rates
my deskmate, and as one who is a good deal older than the minister, and who has been in big business and has seen many big business problems solved, I wish to make a suggestion or two to him. I have seen a small plant grow from the stage at which it engaged very few men until it became a large organization, and this was the result of careful business operation.
I would say, if I were in the minister's place, that this problem ought to be solved not so much from the point of view of raising freight rates as by means of the rehabilitation of the railways themselves, by doing that which will give them the chance that they have not had of increasing their freight carriage. And I would do this by opening up the country so as to produce more freight. One has only to travel in order to see the results that follow from such a program. One has only to consider such a railway as the Chicago-Burlington-Quincy, which runs up the valley of the Platte river, passing through forty towns and cities, all rich and thriving communities. That resulted from the rehabilitation of that area. We have distances two or three times greater in western Canada, and we might have not forty or fifty but sixty new cities and towns which would all produce so much more freight.
That is one of the requisites of our railways. We must produce more freight, and how can the railways get more freight unless we open up the country, build new communities and expand our manufactures? In this connection, I may say that on some other occasion I shall submit for the maritimes a program which, if carried out, will double the population of that part of Canada in a period of fifteen or twenty years. That would mean a great deal more business for the railways.
These remarks I have made tonight have been offered in the friendliest spirit without any intention of criticizing. I simply wish to have the minister take into consideration the necessary means of increasing the freight potential along our railways and reducing the cost of operation by eliminating long nuisance hauls that get us nowhere. If he would do that it would be all to the good of the country.
As an Ontario man, I think I can speak for the people of this province when I say that in a sense we really live through the co-operation of other parts of the country. There is in Toronto a population of nearly one million, and the men and women in that city are engaged in the production of commodities, the raw materials of which come from outside the city. There is nothing in Toronto from which we can make the things we produce there. We import them into the city and our people
convert them into finished goods. Such a program as I have suggested would mean increased returns for us. It would develop other parts of the country and it would mean more freight for the railways.
That, I suggest, would be a good deal sounder than a large increase in freight rates.
I am not saying that it is not necessary to have more freight revenue at the moment. How it will be done I do not know. I am not advocating higher rates. I am advocating the other program of building up the country and bringing in more people and making more freight.
Earlier in my remarks I referred to the country north of Peace River. I have been through that country, hundreds of miles of it, and it was not easy travelling. Sometimes I went on horseback; much of my travelling was on foot. It is a wonderful country. I would call it the last place in the world for Anglo-Saxons, French-Canadians and people of our stock to settle in. But I am sure you could settle two million people there if you provided the facilities, and that would mean a great deal of freight for the railways. That is what they want-more business and more revenue through increased business. If they had more business they would not have to come here every few years for increased freight rates. My last word will be this; High freight rates will throttle instead of encourage business.

speechtext:
There would be no advantage in my repeating some of the arguments which were presented so ably by the Minister of Transport (Mr. Chevrier) the other day. I should like, however, to say just one word as to the utter futility and inopportunity of this debate under present circumstances. To my knowledge, nobody in this house has denied that the railways need the extra money in order to carry on and grant promised increases of wages to their employees. I am not aware either that any objection has been taken to the recent decision of the government to require the board of transport commissioners to make a thorough investigation into the rate structure. As a matter of fact the hon. member for Royal, when questioned by the Minister of Transport, admitted that both steps were justified.
If the complaints of the maritime and the western provinces in regard to freight rates are justified, as I believe they are, this is solely on the basis that, because of numerous considerations which have been placed before the house repeatedly during the course of this debate, historical and economic considerations, they should have lower freight rates than the central provinces. In my opinion that is the problem in a nutshell. That principle was recognized some twenty years ago as far as the maritime provinces are concerned. At that time the Duncan commission recommended lower preferential freight rates for the maritimes, and in 1927 those recommendations were implemented by means of the Maritime Freight Rates Act, which established rates 20 per cent below standard on the bulk of the traffic. This preferential rate has endured for more than twenty years. Whether or not it is still equitable under present circumstances, I am not in a position to say. I would venture to suggest, however, that it is no longer equitable, and that the preferential should be increased to at least 30 per cent below standard. If that were done, according to my calculation the recent increase would amount to only about five per cent as far as the maritime provinces are concerned, and I presume there would be no particular objection to such an increase.
Let me repeat that in my opinion the only consistent attitude for maritime members to take on this matter of freight rates is to press for a further reduction under the Maritime Freight Rates Act. This should be done by way of amendment to the act, not through this ill-timed non-confidence motion. What bothers me with respect to the criticism of the hon. member for Royal is the fact that the situation of which he complains is not a recent development. The hon. member has been in this house since 1935; as a matter of fact he was the only Conservative member returned from the maritime provinces in that election. Not having been here as long as the hon. member, I do not know what if anything he has said or done in the past on the floor of the house with regard to having maritime freight rates further reduced. This argument applies also to the other opposition members from the maritime provinces, though not to the same extent since they have not been here so long. However I do not recall any great pressure being exerted since 1945 by those hon. members with a view to having freight rates in the maritime provinces further reduced.
This afternoon the hon. member for Charlotte (Mr. Stuart) made an interesting suggestion, to the effect that manufacturers throughout Canada should sell their products at a uniform price delivered to the consumer in any part of Canada. He pointed out that this is being done now by some industries in the maritime provinces. I wmnder how many of our good friends from Ontario, particularly on the other side of the house, would do something to promote this suggestion. I dare not venture an opinion as to the extent to which it might be practicable. Possibly it might be adopted in reference to commodities in which the freight rate bears a low ratio to the value; but if it came to coal and lumber and steel I doubt very much whether the suggestion could be carried out.
In any event, if there are grievances in the maritime provinces, as I believe there are,
Freight Rates

I repeat that the solution is a further reduction of freight rates in the maritime provinces. In my opinion it would be the quintessence of irresponsibility for a government to interfere with the judgment of a judicial body set up some forty years ago, with which thus far no government has dared interfere. There would be no more justification for the government to interfere with a judgment of the board of transport commissioners than there would be for it to interfere with a judgment of the Supreme Court of Canada.
For these reasons, Mr. Speaker, I shall have no hesitation in voting against both the amendment and the subamendment.

maintopic: FREIGHT RATES-INCREASES ORDERED BY TRANSPORT BOARD-AMENDMENT, MR. COLDWELL- SUBAMENDMENT, MR. BRACKEN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to add my voice to those who have spoken in opposition to the imposition of a 21 per cent increase in freight rates. I was astounded to hear the decision of the transport board to allow this increase, but I was even more than astounded when I learned the government intended to disregard the request of seven premiers that the federal government stay the order of the board for thirty days until they could make their representations. I feel that this was a betrayal of the democratic principles of this country. At this time, when we are trying to promote peace and unanimity across this country, I think it was poor judgment on the part of the government to permit an action of this kind which imposes real injustices and inequalities upon certain sections of the country. The increased freight rates will make it necessary for many of our labouring people to demand new wage increases, because British Columbia, the three prairie provinces and indeed the maritime provinces will all find the cost of living going up, due, both directly and indirectly, to these new freight rates.
I do not say that there should not be a thorough investigation into the question of freight rates, or that the railway companies are not justified in asking for a revision of rates if they are in any danger of becoming insolvent. The hon. member for Restigouche-Madawaska (Mr. Michaud) stated a few moments ago that he did not consider this debate timely. I quite agree that for some hon. members it is not timely, and indeed is embarrassing, but I believe the leader of this group has done the people of Canada a real service in bringing about a debate in this house on the action of the government in upholding the decision of the transport board to increase freight rates by 21 per cent.
In view of what the hon. member for Restigouche-Madawaska has said, I should

like to quote the amendment which is under discussion today. The amendment moved by the leader of this group (Mr. Coldwell) is as follows:
That all the words after the word "that" to the end. of the question be deleted and the following be substituted therefor:
"this house is of the opinion that the failure of the government to defer the imposition of the increases in freight rates recently authorized by the board of transport commissioners is inimical to the best interests of the people of Canada; further this house is of the opinion that the government should reconsider this matter and take action to prevent the proposed increases from coming into effect at this time."
Later on, the official opposition moved a further amendment which is quite in keeping with my own sentiments and which reads as follows:
That all the words after "this house" in the fourth line of the amendment be deleted, and that the following be substituted instead thereof:
"regrets the government's failure to secure the .removal of inequalities and discriminations in the Canadian railway freight rates structure before the imposition of a horizontal increase of twenty-one per cent-an increase which is bound to intensify the aforesaid inequalities and discriminations, and
Further regrets that the government has refused the reasonable request of seven provinces that the imposition of increased freight rates recently authorized by the board of transport commissioners be delayed for thirty days until they could be heard."
I think that is a reasonable request. We should have democracy in this country because that is what we fought two wars for. It is what we have been trying to build up in this country. Before this we have had the premiers of the different provinces coming to Ottawa to attend dominion-provincial conferences and attempt to bridge any gaps which there might be in our Canadian way of life. They have tried to come to agreement with the federal government, so that details of the British North America Act and other constitutional enactments might be threshed out in a democratic way and bring harmony to this country. But here we have action on the part of the government which has aroused anger from coast to coast. As long as I have been in politics I have never known of an issue which has so much aroused the people of my province.
We are not in disagreement with the right of the railroads to demand an increase if they need it, but I want to say first that the whole freight rate structure should have been thoroughly investigated. If further revenue were needed, then it should have been granted on a basis that was fair and equitable across the country. I should like to quote

Freight Rates
the statement made by Mr. Macdonald in his submission to the transport board. Referring to the revenue of the Canadian Pacific, he said:
The Canadian Pacific railway is thus, on our contention, in a position to pay all of its dividends, all its fixed charges and provide all of the $15" 2 million for additions and betterments, and' leave a surplus of almost $10 million.
I listened with great interest to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Chevrier) when he spoke the other day. I thought he was going to give the whole railroad picture, but in my opinion he failed to tell the house one of the most important things. He said nothing about the profits and the surpluses set aside by the companies to provide for the betterments referred to in their submissions.
I agree with the Minister of Transport when he says that we need able men on the transport board if we are to have a proper investigation, but I feel that it does not take great intelligence to realize that, when injustice and inequality already exist in the freight rate structure, by imposing a further horizontal increase on those existing inequalities you simply increase the burden on a large number of people. I know I speak for the farmers and people of Saskatchewan when I say that all we want is fairness and justice. I do not think that is any more than a democratic institution should give to the people.
The cost of living is increasing all across the country. The veteran who is trying to rehabilitate himself finds it more difficult to get along. There have been further increases brought about by the new rate schedule. We find that on the off-lines the new schedules will apply. It will be only on the transcontinental lines that there will not be any increase in freight rates. Next we find that the minimum weight will be 100 pounds. For example, the cost of shipping a crate of eggs will be increased from 35 to 75 cents. This will decrease the income of the women on our farms who have been shipping eggs and milk and cream.
I have listed what I believe are eight important aspects of this situation which affect the western farmer. It should be understood that the western farmers are the greatest consumers of manufactured products in Canada, particularly farm machinery. The special committee on farm machinery which sat in 1937 found that there was a great backlog of demand for farm machinery in western Canada. During the hungry thirties few farmers were able to buy farm machinery and a backlog of about $50,000,000 of demand was built up. Then during the six years of war with large quantities of steel going into war equipment the farmers found themselves still unable to get farm machinery.
I think this is an instance where a large company has influenced the transport board and the government in order unjustly to impose a situation upon the farmers. The demand for farm machinery in western Canada has now reached a total of from $00,000,000 to $70,000,000 a year. These increased rates will mean a tremendously increased cost, and I have calculated what this additional cost will mean to the western farmer.	*
If we estimate the annual requirements at from $60,000,000 to $75,000,000, plus $15,000,000 for necessary replacement parts, this gives a total of from $75,000,000 to $90,000,000. According to the 1937 special committee, 7-4 per cent of the cost of farm machinery is made up of freight. That would mean about $5.55 million each year. If we estimate the freight from distribution centres like Regina to the local points as being one-third of the freight from the factory to the distribution point, we find that the additional cost will be from $1.85 million to $2.22 million. The 21 per cent increase in freight rates will cost the western farmer in connection with his machinery requirements an additional $1.55 million to $1.86 million a year. That is a tremendous amount of money. Here we have the farmers who are operating on a flexible income which has no stability at all put in the position where it is difficult for them to determine when they buy machinery whether their income next year will be sufficient to allow them to pay for it.
The representations made by the railway companies were based to a large extent on the revenue which they expect to get in the future, and it is interesting to note in that connection just what the Canadian Pacific Railway Company did submit to the board. In their submission the Canadian Pacific Railway Company said that their revenue in 1947 would be about $285-4 million. Actually it turns out that their gross earnings that year were $318-6 million, or an additional $34 million. This shows that the Canadian Pacific Railway Company is in a very liquid position, after allowing for fixed charges, income tax, dividends, additions and betterments, and reserves. Again we find a net increase in 1947 over 1946 of $2-1 million. In other words, the net income of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company increased from $20-8 million in 1946 to $22-9 million in 1947.
I consider that the federal government has given the seven provincial premiers who have tried to co-operate with this government a slap in the face. All I am asking is that the government rescind its action and stay the application of these increased freight rates until it
Freight Rates

has heard the representations of the provincial governments. That would lead to co-operation between the provinces and between the people of Canada. If the railways need additional income to pay decent wages to their employees, let them have it on the basis of equality of rates all across this country. We have already had enough of situations that would break the east away from the west, and the west away from the east. Let us now try to build for unanimity and co-operation across this country. If there is a single thing that will cause fresh labour disputes and demands for increased wages and make it more difficult for the veteran and the farmer and all of us to go ahead in this peacetime economy, it is this very action. I think the government was very ill-advised in- taking the action which it did.

maintopic: FREIGHT RATES-INCREASES ORDERED BY TRANSPORT BOARD-AMENDMENT, MR. COLDWELL- SUBAMENDMENT, MR. BRACKEN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the people of the constituency I have the honour to represent in this house, like the people in every part of the maritime provinces, have been seriously perturbed by the judgment of the board of transport commissioners granting the railways a 21 per cent horizontal increase in their freight rate structure. It is for this reason I want to say a word or two in this debate.
I do not think any useful purpose would be served by my referring to and setting forth again the protests that were made by the premiers of New Brunswick, Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Island, all of whom are, I might say, supporters of the Liberal government. Nor do I think it would be of any advantage for me to take up the time of the house by reading the protests that were made by the maritime transportation commission, by the maritime board of trade, by other organizations and by the press of the maritime provinces. All those1 protests have been brought forcefully to the attention of the minister and the government and to repeat them again at this stage of the debate would be merely a waste of time.
I should like to preface what I have to say by quoting from the report of the royal commission on dominion-provincial relations, known as the Rowell-Sirois report, which was made on May 3, 1940. At page 91, volume II of that report, the commission says:
New Brunswick shares with Nova Scotia the unhappy distinction of the longest unfavourable economic history of any Canadian province. The inferior character of many of the province's resources, and transportation and marketing difficulties, have retarded economic progress and created chronically impoverished areas and distressed industries.
This is not a happy or a wholesome picture or a condition that we would like to see eon-

tinue. The maritime provinces complain that, compared with other Canadian provinces, they have a lower standard of living, a higher cost of production and higher marketing costs, and that these unfavourable conditions under which we have laboured have been made worse by the decision of the board which was handed down on March 20, last, In this connection I should like to quote, and to make his words my own, what was said by the hon. member for Queens-Lunenburg (Mr. Winters) in this debate yesterday afternoon. He said, as reported at page 2920 of Hansard:
There is no question that the increase in freight rates will be a severe and adverse blow to the maritime provinces as well as to the west. Even at the old rates it was almost impossible for our industries to put their products on central Canadian markets at competitive prices. To be in a competing position, it was necessary not only to aim at wages more moderate than those prevailing elsewhere but to keep our other manufacturing costs down. What small measure of success we have had indicates that we have achieved both these aims to some extent. Now, however, the higher freight rates place another obstacle in our path. They will tend to make us live within ourselves in an industrial sense more than ever before.
I have no hesitation in saying that the railways of this country must have an increased revenue if they are to carry on. There is no question in my mind as to the need for this being done. I do not intend to give the reasons I hold for having that opinion. These reasons have been given in the house on a number of occasions during this debate. It is not the increase in revenue but the manner in which the board has decided that these revenues are to be obtained to which objection is taken in the maritime provinces.
A memorandum of the maritime transportation commission on the judgment of the board of transport commissioners states that the board found a straight percentage increase is the only manner by which general increases can be applied. If that is a fact, then I say it is a most unfortunate state of affairs in the maritime provinces.
I wish to say a word or two about the plan of the government to have the board investigate the freight rate structure of the railways. I was surprised at a statement made by the Minister of Transport (Mr. Chevrier) in this house on April 13 during the course of his speech. He said, as reported at page 2908 of Hansard:
This is a motion to go into supply, and my hon. friend has decided to move an amendment to the motion in order to expound a grievance, something which he has a perfect right to do. But I submit that before that grievance was expounded the government had made the grievance disappear by ordering a thorough and complete investigation into the railway freight struc-

Freight Rales
ture by the only board competent and efficient to deal with the question. The government has moved to have the situation righted by this investigation.
If we can make grievances disappear by referring them to any board, then this country would be a country very easy to govern and it would be a happy land in which to live. But, sir, the only way to deal with a grievance is to face it, and the only way that a grievance can be rectified is to solve it. To refer a matter to a commission and think you will solve the grievances of the maritimes or the west or of any other province in that way seems to me to be utter nonsense. The order in council provides for an investigation of freight rates by the board, and it reads as follows:
Order in council P.C. 1487, approved April 7, 1948: directing the Board of Transport Commissioners for Canada to make a thorough investigation of the rates structure of railways and railway companies which are under the jurisdiction of parliament, with a view' to the establishment of a fair and reasonable rate structure which will, under substantially similar circumstances and conditions, be equal in its application to all persons and localities in the various provinces and territories of Canada.
I must confess that when I read that order in council I was puzzled by it. I failed to understand what it meant, or what powers the board was given under it. I believe now, after making a hurried examination-and that is all I had time for-of the Railway Act, that the wording has been adopted from section 314 of that statute which is headed "Equality as to Tolls" and so on.
This board is not all-powerful. Its powers are limited by the act that created it. The board, under the act, as I read it-I do not profess to be an expert in these matters, and I would ask to be corrected if I am wrong- has no power to fix rates that will assist an industry to develop and function. It has no power to fix rates that will remove handicaps under which many maritime businesses function on account of their geographical situation or distance from central markets. It has no power to fix rates that will develop business in the maritime provinces. It has no power to adopt experimental rates. Its powers are limited, and this move of the government in referring the matter to the board is, in my opinion, a political expedient to put to one side a difficulty the government does not want to face up to.
The senior member for Halifax (Mr. Isnor), when speaking in this debate yesterday, said as reported at page 2957 of Hansard:
I cannot help believing, however, that there has been a slip in the wording of the minister's order. In some of the judgments the board takes the view that it cannot handle questions relating to trade.
Well, sir, if there has been any slip in the order, let the minister have it corrected. In my opinion, however, there has been no slip. The wording was deliberately and carefully made, and the powers of the board are, of necessity, circumscribed.
The royal commission on maritime claims, which was headed by Sir Andrew Rae Duncan and had as one of its members Doctor Cyrus Macmillan who for some time occupied a seat in this house, made its report on September 23, 1926. In its report it refers to the limitation of the board's powers. I propose to read into the record a paragraph from this report under the heading "Scope of the railway commission's functions". I do so because I think it is a matter that should be given further study by the Minister of Transport, by his assistants and by the government. This it what the report says in part on page 24:
In addition, the cases which the maritime provinces have already submitted to the railway commission also raise the question of handicaps arising from the geographical position of their natural products, and their distance generally from central markets. If we W'ere satisfied that under their present power the railway commission could adequately deal, on appeal, with the broader aspect of the maritime cases before them, we would make no further comment.
Previous judgments of the railway board, however, lead us to fear that they will not feei competent to deal with such broad considerations as are still involved in these maritime claims. We cite, in particular, the following extracts from the board's judgments: (volume 13, pages 260-261, application of district board of trade, Coalhurst, Alberta.)
"The board, under the railway act, has no profit and loss responsibility, and its intervention in the matter of rates must, as has been indicated, be concerned with matters falling within the categories of reasonableness and unjust discrimination, and not with a policy of the development of industries through rate adjustments.
(Imperial Rice Milling Company v. Canadian Pacific Railway Company, 14 Canadian Railway Cases, 375.)
"The board has no power to regulate tolls for the purpose of equalizing cost of production, or geographical, or climatic, or economic conditions. (British Columbia News Company v. Express Traffic Association, 14 Canadian Railway Cases, 178.)
"It is not the board's function, as delegated by parliament, to make rates to develop business, but to deal with the reasonableness of rates, either on complaint or of its own motion . . . As it has not been established that the rates as charged are unreasonable, the board is not justified in ordering the installation of the experimental rates asked for."
The report goes on:
The conclusion to be drawn from these extracts seems to us to be that the railway commission does not feel itself empowered to pass under its review, when appeals are made to it,
Freight Rates

the same wide range of business considerations which railway companies themselves can take into account in forming a judgment as to the extent to which they should develop trade and business.
The report goes on to state:
At present the work of the railway commission is circumscribed within the two considerations, viz. (a) reasonable compensation to the carrying company, and (b) no unfair preference or unjust discrimination as between traders.
The report then refers to section 320 of the Railway Act which, it says-
. . . seems to give the wider powers that we have in mind to the railway commission, so far as the question of undue preference or unjust discrimination may be involved.
It quotes the section. I am not going to do so, but I have compared the section as set out in their report with the section as it appears in the act as it now stands, and I may say there is no change. It quotes the section and says:
Even there we feel that, if the intention was to have larger national interests in mind, the section should be made clearer, and instead of the words "in the interests of the public" (which might be interpreted as in the interests of the "consuming" public), the words should clearly state that it is national interests (both "producing" and "consuming") that are in mind.
The judgment of the board came before the maritime transportation commission in Moncton on, I believe, April 9; and after considering what the government had decided to do, the commission sent a wire to the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) and a copy of that wire to the Minister of Transport. In that wire it said that the action of the government in referring this matter again to the board was throwing a red herring across the trail. What it had in mind, I believe, when it made that statement were the sections of the act and the powers of the board to which I have just referred.
Perhaps I might take the time of the house to say just what the wire of the maritime transportation commission to the Prime Minister stated. I do not propose to quote it all. It states that in its opinion the spirit and terms of the Maritime Freight Rates Act have been violated, and in addition to that it points out that the effect will be that maritime industry will in many cases, be seriously affected and, in some cases, destroyed. It points out that in using the word industry it refers to agricultural as well as other industries, and then it states:
We feel that the proposal to hold a general freight rates investigation is simply a red herring across the trail. In the very nature of things it will require at least two years-
[Mr. Hazen.j
The Minister of Transport told us it might take a shorter time, six months I believe, or a little longer.
-as did the general investigation of 1925 to 1927, with little or no result.
The wire goes on to say:
We feel that your government should consider the matter outside the railway act because of its economic and political implications. When we consider that seven provinces in this dominion are aligned against this decision and only two are not opposing it, due to their geographical and special locations and their advantages over the other seven provinces in mass production and protection under Canadian tariff, we think you still appreciate the very serious questions that have been raised by this issue.
I think the long and short of the matter is that once these rates are imposed, and they are now imposed, it will be very difficult to get any change. I do not wish to read again the order that sends the matter to the board of transport commissioners, but I am still puzzled and I should like the minister, when he replies, to tell us just what powers the board have, just what they can do after they have heard the matter, and what will be the effect of their decision.

I am still puzzled by one thing, and perhaps the minister can clear this up. I have here a statement made by the Premier of New Brunswick, Hon. J. B. McNair, after the judgment was announced; and in the course of the statement he issued to the press he says:

maintopic: FREIGHT RATES-INCREASES ORDERED BY TRANSPORT BOARD-AMENDMENT, MR. COLDWELL- SUBAMENDMENT, MR. BRACKEN
speechtext:
The discussion arising out of the amendment now being considered, Mr. Speaker, is most important, not only because any change in railway freight rates is bound to have a heavy repercussion on the economic structure of the country, but also because it forces upon us once more the fact of our interdependence with the United States. Because the United States were not successful in applying controls to trade and industry and because political pressure bore too heavily on the Washington administration, controls there were removed, and prices which were already on the way up, skyrocketed to unprecedented levels. Inevitably we felt the shock, because our economies are interrelated, because our importations
affect so many varied lines of business, because so many Canadian goods or machines cannot be completed without the importation of some component parts from the United States. The inflation already existing in the United States rendered so difficult and so complicated the controls of prices here that government advisers decreed that we also should abandon controls. Good excuses were found: necessity to revert to democratic ways and practices; even provincial rights were invoked. The real reason was our dependence on United States economy.
The ruling of the board of transport commissioners that caused the present amendment to be introduced is in direct relation to the removal of controls and the high cost of living, and it will eventually help in raising the latter more. In a moment I will say a few words about the decision itself; but the main object of my remarks is to point out that we adopt, all of us, the attitude of the ostrich when it comes to facing the fact of our economic plight. We did it on the measures for exchange control, for United States dollar conservation, for importation restrictions. We are still doing it.
The trouble is that we have always had a dependent and subservient economy and we carry on, suffering from this condition. We are subservient to Britain and dependent on the British market and the fancies or ingratitudes of British governments, and subservient to the United States and dependent on its price structure, its inflations or depressions. It would not be half as bad if, besides the inconveniences resulting therefrom, we would benefit as much as they do on other occasions and share their prosperity and attain their per capita income.
If we all awoke and realized that stark realities are calling for leadership and courageous decisions we would spend less time in exalting parochialism, in defending east-west forced economy or the long narrow ribbon of railway siphoning goods from the centre to the extremities of the country, and we would start right away to negotiate not only a customs union but a full commercial union which would make all of America north of the Rio Grande an integrated economic unit. We might then still have many of our troubles to face, but we would also have the compensations and the broader life and more rational economy which would result from regulating our trade, not by sentiment or by so-called nationalistic pride but according to geographic, climatic and ethnical conditions.
Under our present fiscal, financial and commercial set-up, this railway problem will always be on us because, over and above the technical and economic problems inherent in
Freight Rates

railways in other countries, we have the problem increased here by the unnatural and artificial pumping of goods across the country at great losses to everyonp. But being as it is and what it is, the railway problem and our economic problems cannot in any way be cured or even helped by the two amendments now before the house. They suggest no remedies. Their result would be only to postpone a needed solution of the problem. I like far more the courage and the logic of the government's decision of not interfering with the railway board's decision.
At this point I should like to congratulate the Minister of Transport (Mr. Chewier) upon the splendid presentation he made on Tuesday last. I do not think he has convinced us that the flat 21 per cent increase constitutes a solution with which all parts of the country should be satisfied, but he has shown the urgency of remedies to be applied, and the great need that the railways be helped at the present moment.
I may say at this point that I have admired the public spirit shown by the members on this side of the house coming from British Columbia, the prairies and the maritimes in supporting the government's attitude and at the same time presenting so well the case for their own parts of the country.
