speechtext:
So far as I am concerned, I think the decision is logical because the matter was entrusted to the board, and the latter investigated the problem at length, coming to its decision after careful study and realization of the seriousness of the situation as well as the impact the increase will have on the Canadian economy. Either the commissioners are not competent or to be trusted, in which case they should be replaced, or they are sincere and sufficiently able, in which case their decision should be accepted. I believe a government should interfere as little as possible with the decisions of specialized, semijudicial institutions; and although it is the duty of the government to review such questions and invoke if necessary the higher motive of the defence of the public interest should any decision be manifestly unfair, I do not think it is right for a government to interfere with the findings and decisions of independent boards functioning under laws created by parliament.
I also think the decision of the government not to interfere with the ordinance or delay its application is courageous, because it is

bound to be attacked and exploited by the opposition parties, who had nothing better to recommend, at a time when its results will be felt by the public. In that connection may I say that not only will the 21 per cent increase be resented by the people, but the small shippers and small manufacturers will be hurt much more than the larger ones. That will come about, not only as a result of the 21 per cent increase, but mainly because of paragraph 5 of the ordinance of March 30, which reads:
The minimum charge for a single l.c.l. shipment between any two stations to be 100 lbs. at first-class rate but not less than 75 cents.
In plain language this means it will now cost just as much to ship orders weighing twenty-five, fifty or seventy-five pounds as it will to ship orders weighing 100 pounds. That may mean it will cost up to 150 per cent more to ship certain goods from one point in Canada to another. For instance, prior to the ordinance it cost fifty cents to ship fifty pounds of tobacco, let us say, from Quebec to Toronto, because I am told that not only are good sentiments exchanged between Toronto and Quebec but also plain goods, including tobacco. Under paragraph 5 of the judgment it will cost $1.21 to ship the same parcel to Toronto. It formerly cost fifty cents to ship .a fifty-pound parcel from Quebec to Montreal, a distance of only 180 miles. Under the new arrangement it will cost eighty-two cents, or an increase of 65 per cent.
That is the part of the ordinance I dislike most, because it is most discriminatory as against the small dealers who necessarily order in smaller quantities. Either the manufacturer will pay the shipping charge and will now refuse to accept orders of less than 100 pounds, or if the dealer pays the freight he is bound to lose much of his profit on goods the prices of which are fixed nationally. This is one of the aspects of the ordinance I consider to be more discriminatory, but there is nothing we can do with the judgment as it is now, or until the new investigation is undertaken.
The .railways are facing a situation that needs to be corrected. The transport board, after long and careful consideration, has rendered a decision. I repeat that in my opinion the stand taken by the government is courageous, and eventually the people will realize that during this discussion no opposition party has proposed any remedy to deal with the railway situation. Delaying application of the ordinance would be no remedy at all. No other party has told us how they would get the railways out of their present predicament in any way other than that decided by the

Freight Rates
transport board. The stand of the opposition parties has been solely an endeavour to embarrass the government and hope for the best. I believe the membership on this side of the house, no matter how much it hates to see these new rates -imposed, no matter how much it hopes discriminatory measures in our railway rate structure, especially those affecting the western provinces and the maritimes, will be removed, will understand that- it is its duty to support a government that shows the courage to uphold an ordinance intended to remedy a dangerous situation. I also hope that the proposed investigation of the rates structure by the transport board may result in an arrangement of rates as satisfactory as possible to all parts and all elements of the country, despite the fact, as I stated at the outset, that our forced east-west economy shall always remain a sore spot in the economic life of this part of North America. I also believe less petty and parochial views are needed before all our economic and financial problems are adjusted.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the other evening the hon. member for Kindersley (Mr. Jaenicke) made a case showing that in some respects the board of transport commissioners were wrong in law in the judgment they handed down. I am not going to elaborate upon his arguments; those interested may find them in Hansard at page 2939 and following. The argument I am going to present this evening is that the board was not only wrong in law but wrong in fact, and that in supporting the judgment of the board the government is equally in error with respect to the facts. I maintain that the Canadian Pacific Railway Company did not make any case at all before the board for an increase in freight rates. I mention the Canadian Pacific Railway Company, because in his judgment the chief commissioner states that the Canadian Pacific has been taken as a guide or measure for the establishment of the rates. That statement will be found at page 36 of the judgment, in these words:
Upon consideration of all that has been placed before us I am of the view that this can best be accomplished by taking the requirements of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company as the guide or measure in the establishment of what we consider to be just and reasonable freight rates to be paid by the users of the railways.
Therefore tonight I am going to refer specifically and frequently to the Canadian Pacific Railway Company, its profit and loss account and its balance sheet, to establish my contention that the company did not make a case at all for any increase in freight rates. On
page 6 of this judgment we find part of the submission of the railway association of Canada:
Canadian railway companies are in the unique and perilous position that they have been operating under rigidly controlled freight rates in the face of steadily mounting costs . . .
That is quite a rhetorical statement, because I do not know what a "unique and perilous position" can be as far as the railways are concerned at this moment. But unfortunately it is only half the truth, and therefore all the more dangerous. I grant that costs have increased, in some respects considerably; but if costs have increased, revenues have increased even more. For instance, at page 11 of the judgment we find a table showing the total operating revenues of all Canadian railways. According to this table, in 1939 total operating revenues were some 8367,179,095, while in 1946 they were $718,501,764, or an increase of almost 100 per cent.
The other evening in this chamber the minister fell into the same trap and only told half the story. He told us about the Canadian National Railways, and that there was an over-all increase, with respect to wages and materials, of 40 T per cent between 1939 and 1946. He did not at the same time tell us about the total operating revenue of the Canadian National Railways, which increased in the same period by some $179,000,000 or the difference between $173,000,000 and almost $352,000,000. When those figures are placed side by side they shed a different light on the situation.
On page 7 of the judgment, paragraph 3, we find the following statement by the railway association:
The decline in railway gross earnings which commenced to be substantial in the latter part of 1945 has progressively continued into 1946 and such decline has not nearly been matched by a corresponding decline in working expenses.
A table is given here by the commissioner, showing that to some extent there was that decline but that the decline was more than made up in 1947. It may be that the railways had reason to fear a decline in 1946, but I think the board might have taken into consideration the substantial increase in operating revenues in the following year. One of the arguments presented by the commissioner, I presume to support his judgment, is to be found on page 11. This is another table showing the total operating revenue, and I quote from the judgment:
From the above it is noted that the monthly percentage increase in railway operating revenues in 1947 over the same period of 1946 is showing a tendency to disappear altogether.
Freight Rates

I assume that he came to that conclusion on the basis of a comparison between November 1947 and November 1946, which showed a percentage increase in 1947 of total operating revenues of only -98 per cent over 1946. Nevertheless, had the commissioner gone back to February of that year, he would have found that there was actually a decrease, not an increase, in 1947 over 1946 amounting to -92 oer cent. But in the ensuing months that decrease diminished and became a substantial increase amounting to 20-05 per cent in May of 1947 as compared with 1946.
Another statement which has been made is that the railroads were suffering from the effect of increased wages which had been demanded by the employees. I do not consider that to be a good argument, and I intend to use some statistics which were taken from the annual report of the Canadian Pacific and also from exhibits 22 and 116 which were presented to the commission. We find that in 1933 the gross operating revenue of the Canadian Pacific was some 8114,000,000, while the wages charged as operating expenses amounted to some 858,000,000, or 51 per cent. This percentage of wages in following years was as follows:
Per cent
1937	 49
1939	 47
1946		 47
1947		 49
I have taken the Canadian Pacific estimate of its gross operating revenue for 1947. This was given as $285 million, whereas the actual figure was some $318 million. Therefore I maintain that the percentage of wages to gross operating revenue would be somewhat lower than 49 per cent. The argument that wages are responsible for the increase in freight rates is one which is obviously not tenable.
On page 9 of the judgment the commissioner asks this question:
Have the applicant railways made out a case of financial need for greater revenue requiring a general advance in freight rates?
He comes to the conclusion by somewhat devious logic that they have. I am going to suggest that the commissioner has altogether omitted facts and has devoted himself to fancies. On page 11 we find this interesting statement:
A close analysis of the current operating revenues of Canadian railways indicates that lower levels may, perhaps, reasonably be expected.

He then goes on to give reasons why he thinks the current operating revenues may be lower, but I am not going to deal with them. Surely this is not a matter of fact. It is a matter of opinion, and I am going to suggest that the commissioner has come to his conclusions on the basis of his own opinions and not on the basis of facts. He is indulging in prophecy when he says that the current operating revenues "may perhaps, reasonably" be expected to be lower. Had the government wanted an opinion like that it would have been much cheaper if it had gone to a teacup reader. It would have got precisely the same answer. Surely that is no basis upon which to establish the case which has been presented to us.

That statement shows the Canadian Pacific's net operating income, after adjustments made by the board of transport commissioners. We are told1 that the net railway operating income, as shown by the Canadian Pacific Railway Company, is $22,892,189. Then the commissioners proceed to add back, and rightly so, certain charges amounting to $6,400,000, arriving at a subtotal of $29,292,189. They deduct for the time being fixed charges, which are added back later. There is also deducted the entire income tax which the Canadian Pacific Railway Company has charged against operation, and the figure arrived at is $25,877,950, on which the board proceeds to compute the income tax. That is an extraordinary situation indeed, where we have income tax accepted as a charge against the operations of any *concern. I should like to know what the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. McCann) thinks of such behaviour. Certainly I know that no business in this country would be entitled to charge income tax against profit and loss account as a charge against the business of the year; but on page 22 of the judgment the commissioner states:
Income tax payable in respect to railway operating income is, I think, properly chargeable to railway operating expenses.
It is a good thing the commissioner said "I think", because obviously from the point of view of business practice it is entirely and completely wrong. Income tax is an appropriation of profits, neither more nor less, and has nothing at all to do with the running expenses of the business. However, it has been added back here, and I shall amend it myself later.
The fixed charges are also added back, leaving a net railway operating income as adjusted, in the mind of the commissioner, at $32,607,841. I maintain that that figure is utterly and completely fallacious.
If that is the basis for the board's action and the government's action, then it is time to reconsider the position. I am going to suggest that there be added back to that figure the $9,057,283 charged for income tax, which would then bring the net railway operating income up to $41,665,124. I am also going to suggest that the "other income" of this railway company be added back in its financial statement, that is "other income" of $24,788,927. When that is rightly and correctly added back we find that the profit position of the Canadian Pacific Railway should be not this $32,000,000 for 1947 envisaged by the board of transport commissioners but $66,454,051.
Let us consider that amount in view of what the board considers to be the requirements of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company. The requirements, as estimated by the board, are $52,332,174. On the basis of my argument, which I maintain is right in law and in logic, the railway company has a surplus then of over $14,000,000. But let us consider how this $52,000,000 is made up. Dividends amount to $21,310,000; fixed charges, $15,787,174; allowances for surplus, whatever this may be, $15,235,000, or a total of $52,332,174.
Let us now see what the chairman of the board of transport commissioners has to say, on page 26 of the judgment, about this surplus:
The question should, I think, be approached from the point of view of whether or not the
Freight Rates

railways are entitled to earn a reasonable surplus over and above fixed charges and dividends and not as to whether provision should be made for a sum to cover specifically additions and betterments. The amount which a railway may consider expedient to expend on additions and betterments may vary substantially in different years.
Of course it may. But what is the effect of this $15,000,000 when added to the requirements of the company? It is simply that an amount equivalent to practically 70 per cent of the dividends is to be credited to profit and loss account, and this may be paid out in some future year as dividends whenever the financial position permits. In other words, what the chairman of the board suggests is that the dividends of the ordinary Canadian Pacific stock should not be five per cent but eight or nine or even ten per cent.
I agree that it is reasonable that some surplus should be appropriated for balance sheet purposes, but I think $15,000,000 is out of the question entirely. A more reasonable amount would, of course, be S5,000,000, in which case the argument of the board of transport commissioners again suffers somewhat, because the requirements of the railway are not $52,000,000 but $42,000,000, and it then has a surplus over these requirements of some $24,000,000.
It has been argued that this $15,000,000 should be used for betterments of the railway and capital improvements. That, I maintain again, is a fallacious argument. This amount is being credited to profit and loss account, no matter how the funds are used. Nevertheless the amount will always be available for distribution as dividends. Whenever the directors of the company think the company needs money for capital improvements, let them go out on the open market and borrow the money for that purpose. As a matter of fact, from the figures I have already submitted on the reserves-and I repeat them again, reserves and unadjusted credits were $91,000,000 in 1939, and are $3S0 million today -the Canadian Pacific Railway Company has lots of surplus fat on which it can live for some time to come.
On this question of "other income" which seems to have perplexed the board of transport commissioners, they saw no reason for adding "other income" to the entire income of the corporation. Surely the board must have forgotten that much of the income which goes under the name of "other income" was derived from gifts and presents of the people of Canada to the same railway system. For instance, in British Columbia-the hon. member for Comox-Albemi (Mr. Gibson) may be interested in this; I expect he knows it-when the Canadian Pacific railway was built in that

province, over $100 million was paid to it in cold cash plus about twenty miles of land on either side of the railway all through the province. That gift is today returning handsome dividends; yet the commissioners refused to credit the revenue from this gift to railway operations.
Then again the company has invested money in various operations. The money that has been invested has certainly been taken from the operations of the company, from the surplus earnings of the company, and therefore any earnings from such investment should be credited to the operations of the company.
We have, for instance, the case of the Consolidated Mining and Smelting Company. I have no doubt that the Canadian Pacific Railway Company purchased shares in the Consolidated Mining and Smelting Company for the purpose of facilitating control of freight traffic. It has paid them handsomely from the point of view of their traffic receipts. This stock is in the books of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company at $8,412,500. Its market value today is about $150 million. Where is this perilous position which the Canadian Pacific Railway finds itself in with all these hidden reserves tucked away?
What about the hotels? Does the board of transport commissioners intend to argue that hotels are not part of the railway business, in view of the fact that the Canadian Pacific Railway Company itself has argued before two courts in this country that legislation affecting hotels is railway legislation? The company cannot have it both ways. Either it is railway business or it is not. If it is railway business then, of course, the proceeds should go into the general fund, as indeed they do. I maintain that when we look at the company's financial position we should consider its overall position rather than the financial position of only one part of the undertaking.
On page 23 of the judgment we find this:
The Canadian Pacific has a common treasury for all its various enterprises and into which goes its whole corporate revenue, including railway operating income and "other income." And from this common treasury all disbursements are made.
In effect, the company makes no distinction at all between operating income and "other income." Farther on the commissioner states:
The whole enterprise of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company is somewhat closely integrated.
Surely a classic understatement.
And for this reason I have found considerable difficulty in appreciating the true situation of the company in respect to its railway operations.

Freight Rates
The commissioner has difficulty; the commissioner never saw through it, and yet he comes to his entirely unwarranted conclusion. Obviously, if these activities are transportation activities, then the profits resulting from them should be included in the general profits of the whole business; if they are not, then they are improper investments for a public utility and the Canadian Pacific should get rid of them rapidly. I maintain' that, on the basis of the figures which I have presented to this house, neither the Canadian Pacific Railway Company, the board, nor yet the government has made a case for the increase in freight rates which has been granted.
Much has been made of the demands of labour for higher wages. I am in complete sympathy with these demands. I see no reason why labour should not get higher wages, but it is something approaching hypocrisy when the Canadian Pacific Railway Company professes to be so desirous of looking after the interests of its own employees in view of its record in the past with respect to these same employees. I am willing to say this. If, after the increases which the workers have asked for have been granted, the railways then show that they are taking a loss, I can see no reason at all why they should not be given an increase in freight rates. But I do not see why they should be given that increase when obviously they are not taking a loss and all they are doing is crying "wolf" and trying to frighten everybody.
Unhappily the only people they frighten are the board of railway commissioners and the present government, and the people of Canada have to suffer for it. So far as we in the west are concerned, even if there is an increase in freight rates, we are not going to lie down under the discrimination which exists in rates as between the west and the central provinces.
Again I join with those who do not blame the central provinces, but discrimination is a fact that has to be dealt with. We in the prairies have to pay 15 per cent more in many cases, in British Columbia and Alberta sometimes about 25 per cent more. Taking the picture by and large over the last twenty-nine years, we find that the Canadian Pacific Railway Company in its western lines has made net earnings of $753 million in the west, and in the east, $361 million, and now it wants to come and soak us once again.
I maintain that the action of the government in what it has done, in passing that order in council, has been hasty and arbitrary and that the Canadian Pacific Railway Company has more than enough tucked away in
profits and reserves to last for two years, no matter what increases are given in wages, until we have the new examination completed. There was no reason for increasing the rates. What we see again is the west, and, I suspect, the east, being exploited, with the active assistance of this government.
We also have the interesting, not to say anomalous position of some Liberal members who were breathing fire and smoke and bellowing loudly against the judgment on the 5th of April, when there was no want of confidence motion before the house. Then they were ready to do anything, but when the chips were down, in true Liberal style we could not see them for smoke.
It reminds me of what Heywood Broun said about a Liberal. As he was walking in Central park with his son, a small boy, they came to a merry-go-round. The youngster began squalling when Broun put him on the contraption and it began to spin around. He squalled more loudly and fiercely until his father took him off and they started away. Then the boy squalled the loudest. He wanted to go back; but he did not want to climb on again, but to stand as close as he could to the whirling thing without touching it and, above all, without having it touch him. "At that moment", said Broun, "I knew what a Liberal was".

speechtext:
There have been so many speeches in this debate that a few more will be in order. The speeches have taken a variety of turns, running from the one the Minister of Transport (Mr. Chevrier) made when he attempted to defend the government's position and tried to make the defence look like a major attack.
There have also been some pretty good analyses of railway statements, and there have been some careful criticisms such as that which has just been given by my hon. friend the member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Stewart).
I am going to try to deal with the matter from the ordinary citizen's point of view as it affects those of us who live by virtue of the work done in our day-to-day occupations, in the west, and to whom the matter of increased costs is extremely important. I know that those who live in the higher realms of finance and business can nearly always take a pencil and balance sheet and justify any action they wish to take in order to improve the position of the particular institution in which they are interested.
It is not by any means an odd situation that they should want to do so, but I sometimes think they do these things without realizing
Freight Rates

the effect on other people, and a great many people will suffer more than they need to because of this action.
I am not going to blame the railway companies very much. After all, they are human beings like everyone else; their interests are in the business they manage, and they attempt to manage that business in line with their particular economic gospel, to get all the profit the traffic will bear. They are not alone in the worship of that particular golden calf.
A number of statements have been made here-I believe someone called it "slick", or used some similar adjective-describing the move which the C.C.F. made when our leader moved the amendment on going into supply the other day. Prior to that, and before the time when these rates were to go into effect, an attempt was made, by moving for the adjournment of the house to discuss the matter, to persuade the government that they should stay proceedings. It was not asking the government to disallow the increase. It was not asking the government to take any other position or to do any other thing than simply to delay or to put a stop to proceedings until such time as everyone concerned had had an opportunity to present to the government the effect which the increase would have on the people to whom they were responsible. These were the premiers of the seven provinces which are affected, who knew the temper of their people and the conditions' in their provinces.
As has been pointed out here before, these premiers, these provincial governments are of different political stripes. So when they said they were dissatisfied with the judgment of the board of transport commissioners, they did so in the full belief that they were dealing with the matter, not from the political or partisan point of view, but from the point of view of the effect it would have on their particular provinces.
It has been said in this debate that the C.C.F. and others who were opposed to the increase were not giving consideration to the needs of those people who worked for wages on the railways. I have read through the judgment. I will not say I have made an exhaustive study of it, as possibly others have done, but at least I have read it sufficiently to know what is not in it, and I find no place in the judgment which indicates that the increase has been granted by the board, in any part whatsoever, specifically to be applied to an increase in wages or salaries of the workers on the railways.
I am also informed by other sources outside the judgment that the unions who represent

the workers on the railways were not permitted to add their voice one way or the other when evidence was being given before the board. I wish further to point out that there has been no alternative proposed by either the government or the board, or by the management of the railway companies themselves. It may be possible that there are alternatives, but if their need for increased revenue was great, alternatives could have been proposed, and they have not been mentioned.
I wish to point out another thing before I go very far into this subject, and that is that in the early stages of the discussion the hon. member for Lethbridge (Mr. Blackmore), who was quite vehement in his observations, pointed out that a thing of this kind, added to the many other discriminatory practices against the west and the east-he was dealing mostly with the west and I will, too-may possibly cause in the west a serious rupture of good feelings toward the two central provinces. The leader of our party said more mildly that it was a threat to good relations, because the country, economically, was bound together by bands of steel. That has been mentioned on more than one occasion both in histories of this country and in historical novels written by people who write things of that kind.
The hon. member for Calgary West (Mr. Smith) was inclined to feel that the hon. member for Lethbridge did not add anything to national unity by making the suggestion. But I think the hon. member for Lethbridge did a good job in doing that, for this reason. While I am the last one who wants to see any disunity, I do not think we should shut our eyes to anything that may happen to cause breaches such as he suggested. I know the people in the west are not thinking of secession-that is, not a large number of them-although it is true that there are a few here and there who will get up and say that we should have secession. But I know there are quite a number of people in the west who, whenever something like this happens that affects them, will then start to consider seriously the suggestion of these few other people I just mentioned who call for secession. I know, however, that the great bulk of the people in the west want to have a united nation in Canada as well as a united nations organization in the world. I am also one of those, and I certainly will never do anything I can avoid doing that will cause any serious talk of a split in our Canadian nation. I think it would be most unfortunate.

Freight Rates
The hon. member for Waterloo South (Mr. Homuth) is, I believe, quite ill. I regret that, and I should like to say to him, through his friends, that I hope his recovery will be rapid and complete. I regret greatly that he is absent because of his illness. But he mentioned the fact that he did not think any differences which might exist between the central provinces and either of the extreme ends of our country were bred entirely of selfishness, and that he believed that it was not fair for him to be able to buy a Chevrolet car-I think that was the example he mentioned-more cheaply than somebody in Regina, Edmonton or Vancouver could buy it, just because there was a heavy freight charge on it out there. I give the hon. member credit for that, and I believe he meant what he said.
I hope his friends will convey that to him because, when he was making that statement, he said that members of this party never had a kind or pleasant word for anybody. I assure him and many of his group that many times we believe in their sincerity. I believe he would do as he says. But unfortunately the history of the country has made it possible for concentration of control of our economic life to be in these central provinces; and sometimes the management of these large concerns which have that control have not exercised the restraint they might have exercised in their dealings with other parts of the country, thus causing to a large extent those feelings which I have just described, which were mentioned by the hon. member for Lethbridge.
We do not want any secession. We want a complete and unified nation. I do not intend to go beyond that as did one member on the other side of the house tonight, I believe, when he suggested that we should have customs union and possibly political union with the United States. I am still quite happy to be a Canadian, and I believe that Canadians can run their own business in their own way without any joining up with somebody else to run their domestic affairs.
With regard to some of the things dealt with by the judgment, there has been misinterpretation either by the press or by political speakers, and possibly a combination of both, which has given rise to a belief that is not correct. We were led to believe that there was to be no alteration in the freight rates on grain. When we read the judgment we see that that is not a correct statement. But the word went across the country making many people believe that it was so. Now we
find ourselves flooded with protests because the new freight rates are being applied on out-of-line hauls, I believe on storage in transit and on local movements of grain in the provinces. That will have an effect on the cost of living and the operations of farmers in both buying and selling their grain in the different localities. I believe these rates should have been left as they were. Of course I do not think any of the increases should have been granted at all in the judgment. But if they were to be granted, I believe that these rates should have been left as the word went out they were to be left.
Another thing I wish to point out is that, as stated in one place in the judgment, the minimum charge of seventy-five cents per 100 pounds on less than carlots will mean, in some cases, not a 21 per cent increase, but more than 100 per cent increase. We will take the matter of a crate of eggs, for instance; and many small poultry people, in order to have their eggs go forward to market as fresh as possible, must ship them frequently in one-case lots. I want hon. members to realize that a great many people operate on a small scale. That is how they make a living, and that living is important to them. I presume that if you ship a case of eggs now under what the judgment has allowed the railways, where it used to cost thirty-five cents to ship a case, it will now cost seventy-five cents. That is more than double the price charged before, and I think it is completely unwarranted and unfair treatment of the kind of producers I have just mentioned.
There is another thing. I am sure that in the judgment I can find no authority for this being done but I am informed that it is being done, and that is-

But what I want to mention now is the matter of retroactive charges on these freight rates. That is not allowed in here that I can find; yet I am informed that in the western provinces, cars that were shipped out before April 8 and were in the showrooms, and farm machinery that was in the warehouse, now have added to their cost the 21 per cent

increase in freight. Who is to get that? Not the railroad. The machine companies and the automobile manufacturers or the dealers will not collect that retroactive freight and turn it over to the railroads.

maintopic: FREIGHT RATES-INCREASES ORDERED BY TRANSPORT BOARD-AMENDMENT, MR. COLDWELL- SUBAMENDMENT, MR. BRACKEN
speechtext:
I agree with the minister. I heartily censure him for not having taken steps to see that no dealer in these machines made that charge on goods shipped before April 8. The government took no such action to protect the people. It did the same thing in this connection that the Tory government did many years ago when it put the excise tax [DOT] on sugar and allowed people with warehouses full of sugar to reap that extra profit and put it in their own pockets. The government has not given the attention to the needs of the people that it should have given.
A short time ago I said no thought had been given to the alternatives. There are at least three principal reasons why the railways felt it was necessary to ask for this increase in freight rates. The first is the tremendous overcapitalization, particularly of the Canadian National; and I want to quote authorities for that statement. First I refer to the report of the royal commission, commonly known as the Duff commission, at page 30:
Another aspect of the problem is the total capital liability of the system. At December 31, 1931, the long term debt of the Canadian National Railways due the public (funded debt unmatured) amounted to $1,276,457,207. The money invested in the original government railways, loans by the dominion government to the privately-owned railways now absorbed in the system, loans to the Canadian National Railways to meet annual deficits, interest accrued on these loans and unpaid, and deficits on eastern lines, together total $1,393,469,164.	The
total of these two sums is $2,669,926,37.1.
It has been suggested that in view of the excessive capital liabilities in relation to the earning power of the system they should be reduced to an amount w'hich would more nearly approximate the earning power of the railway. The net operating income (i.e. the amount available for interest and dividends) of the Canadian National system for the period 1923 to 1931 inclusive averaged $24,414,447 per annum. This figure would require adjustment if adequate provision were made for depreciation. It is obvious that on this basis of earnings the capital liabilities would require a very drastic writing down.
And while this commission is of opinion that it must be frankly recognized that a very substantial part of the money invested in the railways comprised within the Canadian National system must be regarded as lost and that its

capital liabilities should be heavily written down, they do not consider that the time is opportune to deal with this important matter.
That was back in 1931 or 1932. When is the time to be opportune to do that job? Again, at page 86 of the judgment of the board of transport commissioners just issued, they confirm that statement in the second paragraph under the heading "Other income":
The Canadian National Railways are efficiently managed but are operating under a very large debt which carries a large fixed charge, which makes it very difficult to operate from a profit point of view, it being an amalgamation of a number of non-paying roads.
More could be quoted along this line. At page 41 of the book "The Tragedy of Henry Thornton", the writer makes this statement:
It is true that "surgical operations of the bankruptcy courts" should have lessened the crippling burden of capital indebtedness ....
I am not so sure I would want to recommend a surgical operation of that kind, but I say that, since the Canadian National Railways is a government-owned concern, if that is necessary in order to put it on a paying basis, then the proper thing to do is to write it down to its actual value. Then let the capital, which has no representation in physical assets but which represents the savings of widows and orphans and other people who had a right to expect their investment was safe, be provided for and serviced by all the people of Canada, including Ontario and Quebec. That would be a fairer way and a better alternative than allowing this increase in freight rates, which will have a more detrimental effect upon the people of the west and, I understand, those of the east than they should be expected to bear.
